docs.text: Start Here, Errors, System Functions.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text: This page lists what version 2 delivers, what is experimental, the limits you meet today and what is planned. Nothing under "Planned" exists, and none of it has a date.

docs.title: Delivered in version 2
docs.text:
• Start Here, what's new in v2 and migrating to v2
  • One interpreter, written in Rust, behind the kgpy and kg commands (What Runs Where)
  • Language Additions, including modules; strict mode and lint
  • Errors with positions and kinds and the REPL
  • Compiling Klong to C for the static profile, a subset of the language. It has run with desktop C compilers and, for three examples, on two Raspberry Pi Picos
  • The conformance suite
  • The interpreter for boards and its tools (Native Runtime): building, the serial console, IPC and timers, the management node and porting to a board
  • kdb+ IPC and timers
  • Contributing

docs.title: Experimental
docs.text:
• FPGA kernels: Klong functions compiled to hardware. The U250 runs the moving average, FIR filter and a 32-lane strategy replay.
  • The interpreter on boards: it passes the conformance suite on a desktop and has run the console suite on one ESP32-P4 board (ESP32-P4). Two Raspberry Pi Picos have run it with IPC between them (two Picos calling each other). The status table has the detail.

docs.title: Language
docs.text:
Known bugs, where KlongPy's answer is wrong and the right one is known, are listed once, in Differences from Klong. The same page lists the limits of integer power on lists.

Known limit: a Klong function that calls itself is bounded by the stack of the thread that runs it. Under kgpy, f::{:[x;f(x-1);0]};f(6000) runs and f(8000) gives range error: expression nested too deeply. Under kg the bound is 512 nested evaluations, so f(254) runs and f(255) gives that error; see the section on the interpreter on boards below.

docs.title: PyTorch backend
docs.text:
Details are in PyTorch Backend and Autograd.

  • Floats are float32 on every device, so results differ from the numpy backend in the last digits.
  • A tensor cannot hold :undefined, so an :undefined inside a list differs from the numpy backend.
  • MPS has no float64.
  • .gradcheck needs the CPU device and raises on MPS.
  • .export does not complete for some Klong functions, those that branch on a tensor's value; check the export_error entry of its result.

docs.title: The interpreter on boards and under kg
docs.text:
• Recursion depth on small stacks. The interpreter bounds the depth of nested evaluation and the stack it uses, and reports a range error when either is exceeded. kg allows 512 nested evaluations (--max-depth changes it): f::{:[x;f(x-1);0]};f(240) runs and f(255) gives a range error. The two RP2040 Picos had a 112 KiB stack on RC1. In the board test f::{:[x;1+f(x-1);0]}, both returned 113 for f(113) and a range error for f(114). RP2040 measurements
  • Heap needed to load large libraries. A load reads one statement at a time and keeps functions as their text. On the 64-bit host the management library (.l("mgmt")) needs a heap of about 43 KiB to load; .l("nstat") peaks at about 322 KB. On the RC1 serving Pico, the largest contiguous integer vector measured 6,826 elements after boot and 5,060 after a management call followed by two seconds idle. RP2040 memory measurements
  • IPC on a device has run only on two Picos. IPC between nodes and management-library calls have run on two Raspberry Pi Picos. The ESP32-P4 has run the console conformance suite only (the firmware has no IPC). The host build is tested against an open-source q implementation (PeachQ).
  • One flaky Rust test. data_nesting_is_bounded in native/klong-core/tests/full.rs fails in about one run in ten on a desktop. The cause is not known.
  • The default build of kg does not declare the conformance tags bigint, timers, ipc or desktop, so the suite does not test those areas for it.

docs.title: Interop
docs.text: • IPC has been tested against PeachQ, not against kdb+. The tests that use PeachQ are opt-in (see Contributing).

docs.title: Planned
docs.text:
None of the following exists.

  • A WebAssembly build of the emitted C. The C emitter produces freestanding C99; compiling that to WebAssembly is not built. The WebAssembly import module name of an extern is reserved for it (see Compiling Klong to C).
  • Testing against real kdb+. The IPC code would be run against a kdb+ server and client, which has not been done.
  • CI for the Rust tiers. The GitHub workflows run the Python tests, a linter and the docs build. They do not run the Rust workspace tests or conformance/run.py against the kg binary. See Contributing.

docs.title: The static profile
docs.text:
This page is the reference for the part of Klong that can be compiled ahead of time to C or to an FPGA kernel: every type, every shape and every call target is known before the program runs. It is for someone who writes such a program or needs to know why the checker rejected one. A program inside the profile runs unchanged under KlongPy and gives the same answers when compiled; the differences are few. For the tools around it see Compiling Klong to C; for FPGA kernels see Klong functions as FPGA hardware.

kgpy check prog.kg

checks a program against the profile without running it. Every problem is reported, each with its position, the rule it breaks (the word in brackets) and usually a hint:

prog.kg:3:5: static error: the count of n#a (Take) is not a compile-time constant: the result length would depend on run-time data [const-count]
  f::{y#x}
      ^^^
  hint: the count must be a literal, #a or ^a, or a global that no function assigns

The exit status is 1 if any file is outside the profile. -v lists what was found (entries, externs, globals with their types, each function with the argument types it was checked for); --int64 checks integer constants against a 64-bit kg_int. From Python: klongpy.static.check_file(path) returns a report with ok, diagnostics, functions, globals, externs and entries.

docs.title: Compile time and run time
docs.text:
A program is split by what kind of top-level statement it is.

Top-level statement When Meaning name::{...} or name(p;q)::{...} run time a function to compile, if reachable from an entry name::<any other expression> compile time evaluated once by KlongPy on the host; the result becomes an initialised global name::.extern("symbol";"signature") compile time declares a function the target provides, and names it name export:::{;"key";name;...} compile time the interface of a module file .param(...) compile time declares a global that is an input register of the compiled program .entry(...) compile time marks a function as a C entry point and fixes its argument types .l("file"), .l("file";:alias), .l("file";["a" "b"]) compile time loads another file under the same rules: a module (a file that assigns export) is bound to a name, a classic file is read into the program any other expression error top-level effects have no meaning on the target

Compile-time expressions may use the whole language, including the library, .py and file I/O. That is how tables are built: coef::{...}'!64 runs on the host and the 64 results are emitted as data. Only the resulting value has to fit the profile.

Run-time functions must fit the profile. Only functions an entry reaches are compiled and checked; a function used only by compile-time definitions may use anything. A file with no .entry at all is checked as a library: every function, with arguments of unknown type.

The program must parse at strict level 2 (kgpy --strict=2).

kgpy check and kgpy compile c find the file of a .l the way the interpreter does: beside the file that contains the .l, then in the directories of KLONGPATH (default .:lib on Unix and .;lib on Windows), then in the package library.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
Type C type Notes int kg_int = int32_t (default) or int64_t (--int64) booleans are ints 0 and 1 float kg_float = float (default) or double (--float64) fixed<W,I> int32_t (W up to 32) or int64_t a W-bit fixed-point number with I integer bits; see Fixed-point numbers int[d1,...,dk], float[d1,...,dk] pointer to kg_int/kg_float, row-major every d a compile-time positive integer, rank 1 to 4 str const char * only as a literal argument to an extern

A compile-time value is accepted as a global if it is an int, a float, or a rectangular numeric array. Python ints outside the kg_int range, object arrays, strings, symbols, dicts and functions are rejected with the position of the definition.

A global that some compiled function assigns is state and lives in RAM; one that no function assigns is a constant, lives in flash, and counts as a compile-time constant wherever one is required (a take count, for example).

docs.title: What a run-time function may contain
docs.text:
Group Forms Literals integers, floats, numeric list literals, evaluated lists [;a;b] of same-shaped elements Names parameters (x y z or named), locals, head-destructured names, globals, other compiled functions, externs Arithmetic dyads + - * % (% always gives float), :% integer divide, ! remainder, ^ power, | max, & min Comparison dyads < > =, giving int; ~ match on equal-shaped operands, giving int Monads - negate, _ floor (gives int), % reciprocal, ~ not, # size and ^ shape (arrays only; # is the first dimension), * first, | reverse, + transpose (rank 2), !n enumerate with constant n, , wrap as one-element list Structure a@i index with a scalar or an int array; n#a take and n_a drop with constant n, negative meaning from the end; take is rank 1 only; a,b join; n:+a rotate (rank 1); s:^a reshape with constant s; a:=v,i amend of a rank-1 array with one scalar value and either a scalar index or an index list of known length; other forms are rejected Control :[c;a;b] and its chain form :[c1;a:|c2;b;else]; statement sequences; name::expr to a local or a global Adverbs f'a each; a f'b each-2; f/a over; a f/b over with seed; f\a scan; a f\b scan with seed; f:'a each-pair; n f:*a iterate; p f:~a while Calls compiled functions and externs with all arguments supplied

Rejected, each with a positioned error naming the rule:

  • Anything whose result length depends on run-time data: &a where, a?b find, ?a range, =a group, <a and >a grade (grade has a fixed length but is not in the profile, because it needs a sort routine in the runtime), :# split, :_ cut, take or drop or reshape with a non-constant count.
  • f:~a converge and the \~ \* scan forms (result length unknown).
  • Strings, chars, symbols, dicts, :undefined as run-time values.
  • Functions as values: a function stored in a variable, returned, or passed as an argument other than directly as the verb of an adverb. Projections.
  • Recursion, direct or mutual, including .f.
  • .E, .l inside a function, .py*, channels and every other system function; the top-level .l and the externs a program declares are the exceptions.
  • A variable whose type or shape differs between two assignments, or a conditional whose branches have different shapes.
  • Division of an int by zero when both are constants.

The tables below are generated from the checker's own data, so they cannot disagree with it. Each row and each error has a stable id.

docs.text:
Every rejection is a static error that ends in one of these rule ids.

Rule id Group Rejected strict-syntax Program structure and declarations the program does not parse at strict level 2 toplevel-effect Program structure and declarations a top-level expression that is not a definition or a declaration decl-literal Program structure and declarations an argument of .extern, .entry or .l that is not a string literal signature Program structure and declarations a malformed signature extern Program structure and declarations an extern that cannot be declared (bad or reserved name, declared twice with different signatures) entry Program structure and docs.title: Rules for streaming kernels
docs.text:
kgpy check --streamable reports these as the same kind of error, for a program that is inside the profile but would not take one record per clock cycle in an FPGA kernel (see Extra rules for FPGA kernels).

Rule id Reported when Change stream-loop a loop whose number of iterations depends on the data (While, or Iterate with a count that is not a constant) a pipelined kernel needs a bounded loop: use n f:*a with a constant n, and stop early by holding the value stream-state state that is read and written back through a multi-cycle operation (a float operation, or a division or remainder by a value that is not a constant) a float add, multiply or divide, or a divider, takes several cycles, so the next record has to wait for it: keep that state as an int or a fixed updated by adds, multiplies and constant moduli, or let the host do the accumulation stream-table a data-dependent index into an array of more than 1024 items a random access into a big table needs a memory with one port per access; make the table smaller, or index it with a constant window (x@idx with idx[a][b] = c + a + b is a shift register) stream-block an entry that does more than 4096 element operations per call and is not a sliding window such a call is a block program: the kernel can start a new record only when the previous one has gone through its loops. Write the filter as a window, +/taps*x@idx with the index table k+!w, to stream it

docs.title: Fixed-point numbers
docs.text:
fixed<W,I> is a signed number of W bits, 2 to 64, of which I, 1 to W, are integer bits (the sign bit counts). It is for programs whose arithmetic must be exact and cheap in hardware: an add is one cycle and a multiply is a DSP block. It is written in a signature ("fixed<32,16> -> fixed<64,32>") and made by two conversions that are system functions evaluated by the compiler:

.fixed("fixed<32,16>";x)     :" an int, float or fixed-point value (or array) as that type "
.float(x)                    :" a fixed-point value (or array) as a float "

Reference semantics. The value of a number is raw * 2^-F where raw is an integer of W bits and F = W - I. Every operation is defined on raw, and the interpreter stand-in, the C emitter and the hardware give the same bits (the tests compare them over every pair of fixed<8,4> values and over random values of fixed<32,16>, fixed<64,32> and others):

Operation Result raw a+b, a-b, -a the integer result, wrapped to W bits (two's complement) a*b floor(a*b / 2^F), wrapped to W bits a%b floor(a * 2^F / b), wrapped to W bits; b is not 0 (a zero divisor traps like an integer one); W is at most 32 a<b, a>b, a=b, a~b the comparison of the raw values, as an int a|b, a&b the larger and the smaller raw value _a floor(a / 2^F) as an int (wrapped to kg_int) .fixed("fixed<W,I>";v), v an int v * 2^F, wrapped .fixed("fixed<W,I>";v), v a float floor(v * 2^F), wrapped; nan, and anything beyond a 64-bit integer, give 0 .fixed("fixed<W,I>";v), v fixed-point the fraction bits are shifted (a right shift floors), then wrapped .float(v) raw * 2^-F, exact up to 53 bits, rounded to float in compiled code

Where this is written down once: klongpy/static/fixed.py. The C code (klong_rt.h) uses integers only: a product of two operands of more than 32 bits is computed from 32-bit limbs, so __int128 is not needed and a 32-bit target can use any W up to 64; division is limited to 32 bits because a 64-bit quotient needs a 128-bit dividend. Hardware uses the same integer code (so that equality is by construction), not ap_fixed.

What mixes. Two operands of the same fixed-point type; or a fixed-point operand and an int that is a constant that fits the integer part of the type (x*2, x+1). Everything else is an error with the rule fixed: two different fixed-point types (convert one with .fixed), a float (write the float as .fixed("fixed<..>";0.5) or convert the fixed-point value with .float), an int that is not a constant. :%, !, ^ and the monad % are not defined on fixed-point numbers; x|-x is the absolute value. Reductions and scans of + | & work and wrap like the operators they apply; an int constant seed (0+/x) converts exactly.

Under KlongPy a program that uses fixed<..> runs through klongpy.static.call_entry, which evaluates the typed program on the scaled integers: the interpreter has no fixed-point type. A fixed-point argument is a number or an array (or a klongpy.static.fixed.FixedArray), and the result is a float, or with raw=True the scaled integers that compiled code works on.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
.param("gain";"fixed<32,16>";0.5)      :" name, type, and the value it starts with (0 when omitted) "

declares a global that is an input register: the host writes it between runs and a run reads it. The type is a scalar int, float or fixed<W,I>; the name is defined by .param itself and a compiled function may read it, not assign it (rule param). It is not a compile-time constant, so a shape or a loop count cannot depend on it; a parameter bounds a window only as "use the first p of a fixed maximum": +/buf*(!8)<p. Under KlongPy it is an ordinary global; klongpy.static.set_param(klong, "gain", 0.75) sets it between calls (call_entry reads it at each call). In C it is a field of the instance with a setter, prog_set_gain(p, value); prog_init restores the default. In an FPGA kernel it is a register or, with lanes, a table; see Extra rules for FPGA kernels.

docs.title: Typing rules
docs.text:
Inference is forward and monomorphic. Every expression gets one type from the types of its parts.

  • Literals. An integer literal is int, a literal with . or e is float. A list literal is an array of the common element type (any float makes it float).
  • Atomic dyads (+ - * :% ! | & < > =). Scalar with scalar gives a scalar; scalar with array gives the array's shape; of two arrays the shorter shape must be a prefix of the longer, and the result has the longer shape. Otherwise it is a shape error at compile time. The element type is float if either operand is float; comparisons give int.
  • % always float. :% needs int operands and gives int. ! gives int for two ints and float otherwise.
  • ^ gives int only when both operands are int and the exponent is a non-negative constant; otherwise float. (KlongPy returns an int whenever the result happens to be whole; the profile cannot depend on values.)
  • _ gives int. #a and ^a are compile-time constants.
  • Index. a@i with scalar i drops the first axis. With an int array i of shape S, the result shape is S followed by the rest of a's shape.
  • Conditional. The condition must be a scalar. Branch types are unified (int with float gives float); shapes must be equal.
  • Each. f'a calls f on each item along the first axis; the result shape is [n] followed by f's result shape.
  • Each-pair. f:'a gives [n-1] followed by f's result shape.
  • Constant indices are checked at compile time; one out of range is an error.
  • Over and scan. The accumulator's type is the fixed point of acc = f(acc, item), starting from the first item (or the seed); if it does not stabilise after one promotion step (int to float), it is an error. Scan's result is [n] (or [n+1] with a seed, matching Klong) followed by the accumulator's shape. So ,/a (flatten) is outside the profile: write [n]:^a.
  • Iterate and while. The state's type and shape must be the same before and after the body.
  • Functions are specialised per distinct tuple of argument types and shapes. An entry's argument types come from its .entry signature; everything else follows from call sites. A constant passed as an argument is not a constant inside the function.
  • Globals take the type of their compile-time value. Assigning a different type or shape is an error. An int global assigned a float is an error, not a promotion (state must not change type), and so is a float global assigned an int.
  • Numeric promotion at assignment to a local: the local's type is the join of all assignments to it (int with float gives float); shapes must agree.
  • Compile-time constants are literals, #a and ^a, globals that no compiled function assigns, and + - * :% !, max and min of constants.

docs.title: Things to know when writing numeric Klong
docs.text:
• A leading - negates the whole expression to its right: -2#a is -(2#a), -7!2 is -(7!2). Write (-2)#a.
  • Negative counts mean "from the end": (-2)#[1 2 3] is [2 3], (-1)_[1 2 3] is [1 2], (-1):+a rotates left.
  • Take cycles: 5#[1 2] is [1 2 1 2 1].
  • Scan with a seed returns n+1 items: 0+\[1 2 3] is [0 1 3 6].
  • Joining ints with floats gives floats: [1 2],[3 4.5].
  • Lists need brackets ([1 2 3], not 1 2 3), and a name inside brackets is a symbol, not the variable: write [;a;b].
  • a!b and a:%b are C's % and /: (-7):%2 is -3, (-7)!2 is -1 and 7!-2 is 1. Float remainder is fmod (7.5!2 is 1.5). _ rounds toward minus infinity (_(-3.5) is -4).
  • Evaluation order: the right operand of a dyad is evaluated before the left; call arguments and the elements of [;a;b] left to right. Compiled code keeps this order.
  • Names contain letters, digits and . but no underscore. A Klong name maps to a C identifier by replacing . with _. An extern's C name is not derived from its Klong name: it is the C symbol given to .extern, which may contain underscores.
  • A function reads its parameters, its locals and the globals. It does not see the locals of its caller (KlongPy's scoping is dynamic; the profile's is not). A function literal used as a verb may read the locals of the function it is written in, but not assign them.

docs.title: Host functions and entry points
docs.text:
adc::.extern(symbol; signature)      :" a function the target provides "
.entry(name; signature)              :" a function the host calls "

.extern returns the host function as a value, so a program assigns it. The symbol and the signature are string literals. The symbol is the C function: a C identifier (letters, digits and underscore, not starting with a digit), not a C keyword and not starting with kg_. A signature is params -> result: params is a space-separated list of types (possibly empty) and result is a type or void. Types: int, float, int[N], float[N,M], and str (extern parameters only). Examples: "int -> float", "float[64] -> float", "int float -> void", "-> int" (called as name()).

A target's functions live in an ordinary module file that declares them and exports them, and a program uses the file with .l:

:" read.kg "
adc::.extern("read_adc";"int -> float")
export:::{;"adc";adc}

:" the program "
.l("read")
x::read.adc(0)

The compiler reads NAME::.extern(...), export:::{...} and .l(...) as top-level statement forms and does not run them. The compiler name of an extern a module declares is prefix.name (read.adc); the C symbol is separate, and the generated C declares and calls the symbol. A statement that calls .extern and discards the value is a compile-time diagnostic (rule extern; lint E005).

  • The same symbol declared twice with the same signature is one declaration (the header has one prototype); with different signatures it is an error.
  • export must be written as a dictionary literal, export:::{;"key";name;...}, with string-literal keys and values that are names or numbers: the compiler reads the interface without running the file, so a export that is a variable or a call is a compile-time diagnostic (rule decl-literal). The file argument of .l must be a string literal.
  • In C an extern is a prototype under its C symbol and an entry is prog_<name>; the comment on the prototype gives the Klong name and the signature (Klong name read.adc: int -> float). HLS output rejects externs: the card has nothing to call.
  • An entry cannot be called init, t, size or storage.t (prog_init and the others are generated).
  • .entry needs the function to be defined before it and to take as many arguments as the signature has parameters. A function may have several entries with different shapes.
  • A str parameter takes a string literal.
  • The result of a void extern cannot be used as a value.

docs.title: Running a static program under kgpy
docs.text:
The same file runs under kgpy with Python functions standing in for the externs:

from klongpy import KlongInterpreter

klong = KlongInterpreter(strict=2)
klong.externs["read_adc"] = lambda channel: 0.3
klong.externs["write_pwm"] = lambda channel, duty: 0
klong('.l("examples/embedded/pid.kg")')
klong("step(0.31)")                      # 0.12005

or, in one call each:

from klongpy.static import load_program, call_entry

klong = load_program("examples/embedded/pid.kg",
                     externs={"read_adc": lambda channel: 0.3, "write_pwm": lambda channel, duty: 0})
call_entry(klong, "step", 0.31)          # 0.12005, checked against the .entry signature
  • klong.externs maps a C symbol to a Python callable. It is looked up at each call, so a stand-in can be bound before or after the .extern line runs and replaced at any time. klong.externs.declared (keyed by C symbol) and klong.externs.entries hold what the program declared.
  • A stand-in gets one positional argument per parameter: a Python int for int, a float for float (an int argument is converted), a str for str, a numpy int64 or float64 array of the declared shape for an array. It returns a value of the result type; for void the result is ignored and the call evaluates to :undefined.
  • Arguments and result are checked against the signature on every call: a float where an int is declared is a type error, a wrong array shape a shape error, a wrong number of arguments an arity error, each naming the extern and positioned at the call. Calling an extern that has no stand-in is a system error naming it. An exception raised by a stand-in is a python error.
  • .entry under KlongPy validates the declaration and records it; the function is called as usual. call_entry calls it the way compiled code is called, with arguments and result checked against the signature.

docs.title: Running a static program under kg
docs.text:
kg is the engine without Python, so it has no Python functions to stand in for externs. It defines .extern, .entry and .param with the same checks, the same canonical signature as the result and the same error kinds as kgpy, so examples/embedded/*.kg loads there as it stands. A call of an extern that has no stand-in is a system error that names it. A program that embeds the engine supplies an extern by providing a function under its C symbol (klong_extern_register(symbol, fn, ctx, out_cap) in the C interface, declared in native/klong-ffi/include/klong.h; Declarations::provide in Rust), before or after the program declares it. The provided function is not a global: a program reaches it only through the function that .extern returned, which checks arguments and result against the signature.

Known limits:

  • .fixed is a system error under kg: fixed-point programs need the hosted engine, because the engine's own values have no fixed-point kind. fir_fixed.kg runs under kgpy or compiled.

docs.title: Differences from KlongPy
docs.text: A compiled program differs from the interpreter in a few specified ways: integer width, float width, division by zero, indexing out of range, and shapes that the checker rejects at compile time. They are in one table on the page Compiling Klong to C.

docs.title: What is checked without running the program
docs.text: kgpy check never evaluates anything. The type of a global is known to it when the definition is a literal (pos::0, buf::[0.0 0.0 0.0 0.0]); the value of any other compile-time definition (taps::raw%+/raw) exists only once the host has evaluated it. Such a global is treated as numeric of unknown type and shape, the rules that need a type or shape are applied only where it is known, and the summary says how many globals are in that state. Rules about forms (a rejected operator, a string, a function used as a value, recursion, a system function, a count that is not constant) never need types and are always decided. The compiler evaluates the definitions and then applies the same rules with everything known.

docs.title: Reference programs
docs.text:
examples/embedded/ holds three programs that are inside the profile, each with the results KlongPy gives (.expect):

  • mavg.kg: a moving average over the last four samples; the window and its write position are state.
  • pid.kg: one step of a PID controller that reads a sensor and writes an output through two externs.
  • fir.kg: a 16-tap FIR filter over a block of 256 samples; the taps and the index table are built on the host.

docs.title: Extra rules for FPGA kernels
docs.text: These rules apply only to programs built as FPGA kernels (kgpy fpga source, kgpy fpga build); C does not need them. Klong functions as FPGA hardware shows the flow. A kernel is one of two kinds. A streaming kernel, the default, takes one record per clock cycle when the program allows it. A wrapped kernel (--wrapped) runs the program's C unchanged once per record and is slower.

docs.title: Parameters in a kernel
docs.text: A .param is a register of the kernel (an s_axilite argument). With --lanes N the kernel holds N copies of the program, the N values of every parameter are one table in card memory that the kernel reads when it starts, and .fpga.set fills the table. The host runtime cannot write an array to a register, which is why a table is used.

docs.title: A summary entry
docs.text:
An entry reads or changes the program's state, and every entry of a program works on the same state: under KlongPy the same globals, in C the same instance. A hardware kernel is one entry, so that sharing needs one more rule, for the case where a run feeds many records and reads a small result at the end (a strategy replayed over a tick history, where a result per tick would cost more than the computation).

A void entry with arguments (the driver) and one entry without arguments that returns a value (the reader) form a summary pair. The kernel of the driver makes its n calls, writes nothing for them, then calls the reader once and writes that one result record (with --lanes N, one per lane, lane first). n may be 0: the kernel then reads the state as it is. The reader is not a kernel of its own. Only a streaming kernel can have a summary pair; a wrapped kernel rejects it. A void entry without a reader cannot be a kernel, and a reader without a driver is an entry that takes no argument. Both are [hls] errors that say so.

A complete pair:

$ cat > sum_demo.kg <<'EOF'
> total::0.0
> count::0
> step::{total::total+x;count::count+1;0}
> report::{total,count}
> .entry("step";"float -> void")
> .entry("report";"-> float[2]")
> EOF
$ kgpy check sum_demo.kg
sum_demo.kg: inside the static profile (2 functions, 2 entries, 0 externs, 2 globals)

Every other target does the same by hand: call_entry(klong, "step", x) for each record, then call_entry(klong, "report"), and the C emitter has prog_step(p, x) and prog_report(p, out) on one instance. examples/hardware/crossover.kg is a worked pair.

docs.title: Checking that a kernel can stream
docs.text:
kgpy check --streamable prog.kg answers a second question about a program that is inside the profile: can a hardware kernel take one record per clock cycle? It reports, with the span of the construct and what to change, each of:

  • a loop with a data-dependent bound (stream-loop);
  • state that is read and written back through a multi-cycle operation, a float operation or a division by a value that is not a constant (stream-state);
  • a data-dependent index into an array of more than 1024 items (stream-table);
  • an entry that does more than 4096 element operations per call and is not a sliding window (stream-block).

A sliding window is +/taps*x@idx with the index table k+!w. The kernel keeps the last w samples in a shift register and makes one output per input word.

docs.title: Strict mode
docs.text:
Klong accepts a lot of input that is almost certainly a mistake. 1 2 3 evaluates to 1 and drops the rest. An undefined name evaluates to its own symbol. A function called with too many arguments ignores the extras. Strict mode turns these into errors. It has three levels, and the default is level 0, which behaves as Klong always has.

Level What it adds 0 Nothing is rejected. Input that is probably a mistake gets a warning and runs as it always did. 1 The parser's warnings become syntax errors. A function cannot create a variable by assignment, and cannot read one that is not defined. The left side of :: must be a name. 2 Level 1, plus: reading an undefined name is an error everywhere, :a is always the symbol a, a declared local cannot be read before it is assigned, and a call with more arguments than the function takes is an error.

Each level includes the rules of the one below it. Rules that are errors at every level (an adverb that does not touch its verb, say) are not strict-mode rules and are listed in Errors.

docs.title: Selecting a level
docs.text:
From How The command line kgpy --strict is level 1. kgpy --strict=2 is level 2 (kgpy --strict 2 also, as a lone 0, 1 or 2 after the bare flag is its level). --strict=0 is the default. A level other than 0, 1 or 2 is refused. Python KlongInterpreter(strict=2). The level is the strict property of the interpreter, which can be assigned. Only the integers 0, 1 and 2 are accepted; anything else raises ValueError. Klong code .strict() sets level 1, .strict(n) sets level n, .unsafe() sets level 0. Each returns the new level. 
$ kgpy -e 'a'
:a
$ kgpy --strict=2 -e 'a'
<expr>:1:1: name error: undefined: a
  a
  ^
$ kgpy --strict=3 -e 'a' >/dev/null 2>&1; echo $?
2

from klongpy import KlongInterpreter

klong = KlongInterpreter(strict=2)
klong.strict        # 2
klong.strict = 1    # change it later

In a session, .strict and .unsafe set the level for what runs afterwards:

?> .strict(2)
2
?> .strict()
1
?> .unsafe()
0
?> .strict(3)
error: the strict level must be 0, 1 or 2

A file run with kgpy --strict=N file.kg, and a file loaded with .l, run at the level of the session. The level in force when a text is parsed decides the syntax checks for that text; the level in force when a statement runs decides the run-time checks. The same text can therefore be accepted at level 0 and rejected at level 1 by the same interpreter (the first example under Input that is left over).

The default stays at level 0 so that existing programs keep their results. kgpy lint finds many of the same mistakes in a file without running it.

docs.title: Input that is left over
docs.text:
At level 0 each of these is a warning and the program runs as it did. At level 1 each is a syntax error and nothing is evaluated.

A complete statement followed by more input:

?> 1 2 3
1
?> .strict(1)
1
?> 1 2 3
error: unexpected '2' after the end of the expression

A closer with nothing open:

?> 1+1 )
2
?> .strict(1)
1
?> 1+1 )
error: unexpected ')': nothing is open that it could close

A missing operand:

?> f::
None
?> .strict(1)
1
?> f::
error: missing right operand for ::
?> +/
error: missing operand for +/

A string, list, dictionary or comment that is not closed:

?> "abc
"abc"
?> [1 2 3
[1 2 3]
?> .strict(1)
1
?> "abc
error: unterminated string: the closing " is missing
?> [1 2 3
error: unterminated list: the closing ] is missing
?> :{[1 2]
error: unterminated dictionary: the closing } is missing
?> 3:"x
error: unterminated comment: the closing " is missing

A newline after a comment inside a function body is a separator at level 0, as if it were a ;. At level 1 it is an ordinary newline, so the next line continues the expression:

?> f::{x :"note"
.. +2}
:monad
?> f(1)
2
?> .strict(1)
1
?> f::{x :"note"
.. +2}
:monad
?> f(1)
3

Syntax warnings lists every code and what it does at level 0.

docs.title: The left side of ::
docs.text:
Assigning to something that is not a name stored a meaningless entry at level 0. A name in parentheses, (a)::5, is still a name.

?> 1::5
5
?> "a"::5
5
?> .strict(1)
1
?> 1::5
error: cannot assign: the left side of :: must be a name
?> "a"::5
error: cannot assign: the left side of :: must be a name
?> (a)::5
5

A list on the left of :: is a destructuring when it holds distinct plain names. Any other list was accepted at level 0 and bound nothing; at level 1 it is an error:

?> [a [b c]]::[1 [2 3]]
[1 [2 3]]
?> a
:a
?> .strict(1)
1
?> [a [b c]]::[1 [2 3]]
error: cannot destructure: nested lists are not supported
?> [a a]::[1 2]
error: cannot destructure: a is named twice

docs.title: Assigning inside a function
docs.text:
At level 0 :: on an unknown name inside a function creates a variable that belongs to that call and disappears when it returns. It does not create a global, and .unsafe() does not change that. At level 1 the assignment is an error unless the name is a parameter, a declared local, or already defined.

?> f::{c::1}
:nilad
?> f()
1
?> .strict(1)
1
?> f()
error: undefined variable: c

Declare the name as a local, {[c];c::1}, or define the global before the function runs. To create a global from inside a function, use .E.

?> .strict(1)
1
?> f::{[c];c::1;c+1}
:nilad
?> f()
2
?> total::0
0
?> add::{total::total+x}
:monad
?> add(5)
5
?> total
5

docs.title: Reading an undefined name inside a function
docs.text:
?> g::{a+1}
:nilad
?> g()
error: cannot apply + (Plus) to symbol and integer
?> .strict(1)
1
?> g()
error: undefined: a
?> a::2
2
?> g()
3

At level 1 a name read at the top level that is not defined is still its own symbol: a prints :a. Level 2 closes that.

docs.title: Undefined names
docs.text:
Reading a name that is not defined is a name error, at the top level too. The message carries a "did you mean" hint when one defined name is close to it. The hint uses the names defined in the interpreter and a similarity cutoff of 0.7, so a one-letter slip is caught and a very different name gets no hint. The first example shows the error as the REPL prints it, with the hint line.

?> lenght::3
3
?> lenth
1:1: name error: undefined: lenth
  lenth
  ^^^^^
  hint: did you mean lenght?
?> zzz
1:1: name error: undefined: zzz
  zzz
  ^^^

A failed read defines nothing, so a is still undefined after a+1 fails. Without strict mode, a+1 fails inside the operator, with an error about a symbol and an integer, and a is defined as :a. Calling a function that is not defined is a name error at every level:

?> a+1
error: undefined: a
?> a
error: undefined: a
?> nosuch(1)
error: undefined function: nosuch

docs.title: Quoted symbols
docs.text:
At levels 0 and 1, :foo is looked up as a variable when one called foo exists. At level 2 a quoted symbol is always the symbol. This is what lets a program keep symbols as data, such as the keys of a dictionary or the column names of a table, whatever variables happen to be defined.

?> foo::5
5
?> :foo
5
?> .strict(2)
2
?> :foo
:foo
?> {x}'[:foo :bar]
[:foo :bar]

A name that is not quoted is looked up, and an undefined name is an error at level 2, so :foo and foo are different things. To get the value of the variable, write foo. A list of symbols written [:a :b] is data at every level.

docs.title: Locals read before assignment
docs.text:
A declared local starts out as its own symbol at level 0 and 1. At level 2 reading it before it is assigned is an error:

?> f::{[a];a}
:nilad
?> f()
:a
?> .strict(2)
2
?> f()
error: local 'a' read before assignment

docs.title: Too many arguments
docs.text:
A function takes as many arguments as the highest of x, y and z it uses, or as many as it has named parameters. At levels 0 and 1 extra arguments are dropped. At level 2 they are an arity error. A call with fewer arguments, written f(1;) with the empty slot or f(1) without it, is a projection, and is not an error at any level.

?> {x+y}(1;2;3)
3
?> .strict(2)
2
?> {x+y}(1;2;3)
error: the function takes 2 arguments, got 3
?> f::{x}
:monad
?> f(1;2)
error: f takes 1 argument, got 2
?> {x+z}(1;2;3)
4
?> p::{x+y}(1;)
:monad
?> p(10)
11
?> q::{x+y}(1)
:monad
?> q(10)
11

{x+z} takes three arguments because it uses z, so a call with three is correct. The check also applies to functions called through adverbs and to system functions:

?> .strict(2)
2
?> {1}'[1 2]
error: the function takes no arguments, got 1
?> .p("a";"b")
error: .p takes 1 argument, got 2

An x, y or z inside a nested function literal does not count for the outer function. See how many arguments a function takes.

docs.title: Which level to use
docs.text:
Use level 2 for new code. It reports a mistyped name at the place it is written, not several operations later as a numpy error about a string and an integer, and it catches calls that pass arguments a function never reads. Write new files so that they run under --strict=2 and keep it on in tests.

Use level 1 to bring an existing program under strict checking, because it needs no change to how names are read: what it rejects is input that was already wrong or that never did what it appeared to do. Fix what it reports, then try level 2.

Leave level 0 on for programs written before these levels existed, and for a program that relies on one of the behaviours above. The interactive REPL also starts at level 0.

The standard library under klongpy/lib loads at levels 0, 1 and 2, so a strict program can load it with .l.

Run kgpy lint over a file to see the same kinds of mistake without running anything.

See also: Errors, Conformance Suite (the strict1 and strict2 cases), Migrating to v2.

docs.title: System Functions and Variables
docs.text:
This page lists every system function and variable that KlongPy defines, with a one-line description and the full text of its docstring. It is generated from the eval_sys_* docstrings, and the output shown is what the interpreter prints. The REPL command ]h .name shows the docstring.

An error is shown as error: message, without the position the REPL adds; see Reading an error.

docs.title: Evaluation and output
docs.text: Name Title Description .E(x) Evaluate Evaluate a string of Klong at global scope and return the result. .d(x) Display Display a value without a newline (strings print without quotes). .p(x) Print Display a value followed by a newline. .pf(x;y) Print-Format Fill a template like .fmt, print the result and a newline, and return the string. .fmt(x;y) Format Fill a template string with {} placeholders and return the string. .w(x) Write Write a value in readable form (strings keep their quotes), without a newline. .bkd(x) Backend-Display Display a value in the backend's own format (a torch tensor stays a tensor). .bkp(x) Backend-Print Print a value in the backend's own format, followed by a newline. .x(x) Exit Exit the interpreter with a success or failure status. .l(x) Load Load a Klong file: a module (a file that assigns export) is bound to its name, to an alias or by its entries; any other file is loaded into the globals. .module(x) Module Mark the start or end of a module; .module(:name) opens one and .module(0) closes it. .pc() Process-Clock Return the process time used so far, in seconds. .now() Now Return the time of day in seconds since the start of 1970. .rn() Random-Number Return a random real number in 0 <= x < 1. .seed(x) Seed Seed the random number generator, so the draws that follow are the same on every machine. .sys(x) System Run a shell command and return its exit code. .try(x;y) Try Call a function with a list of arguments and give the outcome as a value: [1 result], or [0 e] where e is a dictionary describing the error. .err(x;y) Error Fail with an error of a given kind and message (the inverse of .try). .mem() Memory The memory the native interpreter uses: bytes in use, the most that was in use, the limit. .ver() Version A dictionary that describes the interpreter: version, integer and float widths, features, platform.

docs.title: .E
docs.text:
.E(x) [Evaluate]

Evaluate the Klong program contained in the string "x" and
return its result. This is a direct interface to the Klong
system, e.g. .E("a::123");a will yield 123.

Evaluation happens at GLOBAL scope, so top-level definitions
(`name::...`) persist as globals, even when .E is called from
inside a function (e.g. runtime code generation). Without this,
new vars would land in the (transient) calling frame and be lost.

?> .E("a::123");a
123

docs.title: .d
docs.text:
.d(x) [Display]

Display the object "x". Backend arrays are converted to numpy for cleaner output.
Use .bkd() for raw backend-specific display.

docs.title: .p
docs.text:
.p(x) [Print]

Pretty-print the object "x" (like Display) and then print a
newline sequence. Backend arrays are converted to numpy for cleaner output.
Use .bkp() for raw backend-specific print.

?> .p([1 2 3])
[1 2 3]
"[1 2 3]"

docs.title: .pf
docs.text:
.pf(x;y) [Print-Format]

.pf(x)

Like Format (.fmt), but also write the result and a newline
sequence to the current output channel. Return the string.

Example:   .pf("a={}";1)   writes  a=1

?> .pf("a={}";1)
a=1
"a=1"
?> .pf("done")
done
"done"

docs.title: .fmt
docs.text:
.fmt(x;y) [Format]

.fmt(x)

Return the template string "x" with its placeholders replaced by
the arguments in "y". If "y" is a list (not a string), its elements
are the arguments; otherwise "y" is the single argument. To pass one
list as the only argument, wrap it: .fmt("{}";,[1 2 3]). A template
with no placeholders may be given alone: .fmt("done") is "done". A
template with placeholders and no arguments is a range error that
counts the placeholders. A list of numbers is an array, so in
.fmt("{} {}";[;3;2.5]) the 3 has already become 3.0 when .fmt sees it.

Placeholders: "{}" takes the next argument, "{0}", "{1}" take by
index (the two styles may not be mixed), "{{" and "}}" are literal
braces. A format may follow a colon, as in "{:8}", "{0:-8}" and
"{:5.2}", and is applied like Format2 (n$value): a positive width
pads on the right, a negative width on the left, and a fractional
format such as 5.2 formats a number (an integer is converted to a
real first). A width pads with spaces: a format with a leading zero,
as in "{:02}", is a range error. Arguments are rendered as Display does.

Examples:   .fmt("Spot: {}";3.5)       -->  "Spot: 3.5"
            .fmt("{1} {0}";[;1;2])     -->  "2 1"
            .fmt("{:5.2}";3)           -->  "    3.00"

?> .fmt("Spot: {}";3.5)
"Spot: 3.5"
?> .fmt("{1} {0}";[;1;2])
"2 1"
?> .fmt("{:8}";"ab")
"ab      "
?> .fmt("{:-8}";"ab")
"      ab"
?> .fmt("{:5.2}";3.0)
"    3.00"
?> .fmt("{{}}";1)
"{}"
?> .fmt("{}{}";1)
error: .fmt: 2 placeholder(s) but 1 argument(s) in template '{}{}'
?> .fmt("done")
"done"

docs.title: .w
docs.text:
.w(x) [Write]

.d and .w both write "x" to the currently selected output port.
However, .w writes a "readable" representation of the given
object and .d pretty-prints the object. The "readable" output
is suitable for reading by .r.

For most types of object there is no difference. Only strings
and characters are printed in a different way:

Object          | .d(Object) | .w(Object)
-------------------------------------------
0cx             |  x         | 0cx
"test"          |  test      | "test"
"say ""hi"""  |  say "hi"  | "say ""hi"""

For some objects, there is no readable representation, including
functions, operators, the undefined object, and the "end of file"
object. A symbolic representation will be printed for those:
:nilad, :monad, :dyad, :triad, :undefined, :eof.

None of these functions terminates its output with a newline
sequence. Use .p (Print) to do so.

docs.title: .bkd
docs.text:
.bkd(x) [Backend-Display]

Display the object "x" in raw backend format (tensors shown as-is).

docs.title: .bkp
docs.text:
.bkp(x) [Backend-Print]

Pretty-print the object "x" in raw backend format (tensors shown as-is)
and then print a newline sequence.

docs.title: .x
docs.text:
.x(x) [Exit]

Terminate the Klong interpreter, returning "success" to the
operating system, if "x" is false (0, [], "") and "failure",
if "x" is not false.

docs.title: .l
docs.text:
.l(x) [Load]

.l(x;y)

Load the Klong file named by the string "x". A file that assigns
the variable export is a module; any other file is classic Klong.

A module runs once, in a scope of its own, and .l returns it: a
read-only dictionary of what the file gave to export. The other
names of the file stay private to it. The module is bound in the
scope that called .l:

    .l("nstat")                binds it to the file's name, nstat
    .l("nstat";:s)             binds it to s instead
    .l("nstat";["mu" "sd"])    binds those entries as names mu and sd

A missing entry is an error that names it. A dictionary entry is
read as m.name, which is m@"name". The stem must be a name (letters
and digits, starting with a letter) or an alias is given. At strict
levels 0 and 1 a quoted symbol :s is the value of s when s is
defined, so give an alias that is not in use.

A classic file is loaded as if typed in at the prompt: its names go
into the globals, and .l returns the last expression evaluated. A
second argument on a classic file is an error.

A name without ./ or ../ is searched in the directory of the file
that contains the .l (the working directory at the prompt), then in
the directories of KLONGPATH (default ".:lib" on Unix and ".;lib" on
Windows), then in the bundled library; a file found before the library that has the name of a
library file is a warning. "x" and "x.kg" are tried in each. ./x and
../x are taken from the directory of the file that has the .l, and
an absolute path as it is.

docs.title: .module
docs.text:
.module(x) [Module]

Delimit a module. See MODULES documentation.

docs.title: .pc
docs.text:
.pc() [Process-Clock]

Return the process time consumed by the Klong interpreter so
far. The return value is in seconds with a fractional part
whose resolution depends on the operating environment and may
be anywhere between 50Hz and 1MHz.

The program {[t0];t0::.pc();x@[];.pc()-t0} measures the process
time consumed by the nilad passed to it.

docs.title: .now
docs.text:
.now() [Now]

Return the time of day as seconds since the start of 1970,
with a fractional part. On a board without a clock this is
a system error.

docs.title: .rn
docs.text:
.rn() [Random-Number]

Return a random number x, such that 0 <= x < 1.

?> .rn()<1
1

docs.title: .seed
docs.text:
.seed(x) [Seed]

Set the state of the random number generator from the
integer "x" and return "x". The draws of .rn() that follow
are the same on every machine and board for the same seed.

Example: .seed(42);.rn()  -->  0.1941059175341826

docs.title: .sys
docs.text:
.sys(x) [System]

Pass the command in the string "x" to the operating system for
execution and return the exit code of the command. On a Unix
system, the command would be executed as

sh -c "command"

and an exit code of zero would indicate success. The command's
stdout and stderr are inherited from the interpreter process. On
Windows the command is run through cmd.

The exit code is returned as an integer. Output of the command goes to the terminal of the interpreter process, not to the Klong output channel, so .tc does not capture it.

?> .sys("exit 3")
3
?> .sys("true")
0
?> .sys("false")
1

docs.title: .try
docs.text:
.try(x;y) [Try]

Call the function "x" with the list of arguments "y" and return the
outcome as a value: [1 result] when the call worked, or [0 e] when
it failed with a Klong error. "e" is a dictionary with the entries
"kind" (syntax, name, arity, type, shape, range, system, memory,
internal or remote), "message", "source", "line" and "col". An
interrupt (Ctrl-C) and .x are not caught.

A function written in place needs no name: .try({risky()};[]).

Examples:   .try({x+1};[1])                 -->  [1 2]
            (.try({x+1};["a"])@1)@"kind"    -->  "type"

docs.title: .err
docs.text:
.err(x;y) [Error]

Fail with an error of the kind "x" (a string or symbol: syntax, name,
arity, type, shape, range, system, memory, internal or remote) and the
message "y", a string. With one argument, a dictionary that .try
caught, .err(e) raises that error again.

Example:   .err("range";"too big")

docs.title: .mem
docs.text:
.mem() [Memory]

The memory the native interpreter uses: a list of three integers,
the bytes in use, the most that was in use, and the limit (0 where
there is none, as on the desktop and under KlongPy).

docs.title: .ver
docs.text:
.ver() [Version]

A dictionary that describes the interpreter: "version" (a string),
"int" and "float" (the widths in bits), "features" (a list of
strings) and "platform".

Example:   (.ver())@"version"

docs.title: Reading and files
docs.text: Name Title Description .r() Read Read one data object from the current input channel. .rl() Read-Line Read one line from the current input channel. .rls() Read-Lines Read all remaining lines from the current input channel as a list of strings. .rs(x) Read-String Read a data object from a string (the inverse of .w). .mi(x) More-Input Return 1 if the input channel has more input, otherwise 0. .ic(x) Input-Channel Open a file for reading and return an input channel. .oc(x) Output-Channel Open a file for writing (truncating it) and return an output channel. .ac(x) Append-Channel Open a file for appending and return an output channel. .cc(x) Close-Channel Close a channel. .fc(x) From-Channel Select the input channel, or restore standard input with a false value. .tc(x) To-Channel Select the output channel, or restore standard output with a false value. .fl() Flush Flush the current output channel. .df(x) Delete-File Delete a file; an error if it cannot be deleted.

docs.title: .r
docs.text:
.r() [Read]

Read a single data object from the currently selected input port
and return it. The object being read may be an atom or a list.
When it is a dictionary or list, the input may span multiple
lines. At the end of input the result is :undefined.

docs.title: .rl
docs.text:
.rl() [Read-Line]

Read a line from the From Channel and return it as a string.
If there is a line separator at the end of the line, it will
be stripped from the string.

docs.title: .rls
docs.text:
.rls() [Read-Lines]

Read all lines from the From Channel and return it as an array.
If there is a line separator at the end of the line, it will
be stripped from the string.

docs.title: .rs
docs.text:
.rs(x) [Read-String]

.rs is like .r, but reads its input from the string "x". It is
intended for converting serialized compound data objects,
such as lists, arrays, and dictionaries, back to their internal
forms. "x" must be a string. Empty or blank text holds no
object and gives :undefined, as does .r at the end of input.

.rs stops after the first object: .rs("7 8") is 7. To read a
number from text and refuse anything else, use .num.

?> .rs("[1 2 3]")
[1 2 3]
?> .rs("7 8")
7

docs.title: .mi
docs.text:
.mi(x) [More-Input]

This function returns 1, if the From Channel is not exhausted
(i.e. no reading beyond the EOF has been attempted on that
channel). When no more input is available, it returns 0.

This is a "negative EOF" function.

docs.title: .ic
docs.text:
.ic(x) [Input-Channel]

Open the file named in the string "x", link it to an input
channel, and return that channel. Opening a non-existent file
is an error.

docs.title: .oc
docs.text:
.oc(x) [Output-Channel]

Both of these functions open a file named in the string "x",
link it to an output channel, and return that channel. The
difference between them is that .oc truncates any existing
file and .ac appends to it.

docs.title: .ac
docs.text:
.ac(x) [Append-Channel]

See [Output-Channel].

docs.title: .cc
docs.text:
.cc(x) [Close-Channel]

Close the input or output channel "x", returning []. Closing an
already closed channel has no effect. A channel will be closed
automatically when no variable refers to it and it is not the
current From or To Channel.

docs.title: .fc
docs.text:
.fc(x) [From-Channel]

.fc selects input channel "x" for reading and .tc selects
output channel "x" for writing, i.e. these functions select a
new From and To Channel, respectively. All input/output will
be redirected to the given channel. Both function will return
the channel that was previously in effect.

When a false value (0,[],"") is passed to these functions, they
restore the default From or To Channel (.cin or .cout).

docs.title: .tc
docs.text:
.tc(x) [To-Channel]

See [From-Channel]

docs.title: .fl
docs.text:
.fl() [Flush]

Make sure that all output sent to the To Channel is actually
written to the associated file or device ("flush" the channel).

docs.title: .df
docs.text:
.df(x) [Delete-File]

Delete the file specified in the string "x". When the file
cannot be deleted (non-existent, no permission, etc), signal
an error.

docs.title: Strings
docs.text: Name Title Description .split(x;y) Split Split a string at each occurrence of a separator into a list of strings; empty pieces are kept. .join(x;y) Join Join a list of strings with a separator between them (the inverse of .split). .words(x) Words The non-empty pieces of a string between runs of white space. .trim(x) Trim A string without its leading and trailing white space. .num(x) Number The number a whole string spells, or :undefined when it is not exactly one number.

docs.title: .split
docs.text:
.split(x;y) [Split]

Return the pieces of the string "x" between the occurrences of
"y", a string of one or more characters or a character, as a list
of strings. Empty pieces are kept: there are as many pieces as
occurrences of "y" plus one, and the split of "" is [""]. An
empty "y" is a range error.

.join is the inverse: .join(.split(x;y);y) is "x".

?> .split("a,,b";",")
["a" "" "b"]
?> .split("";",")
[""]
?> .split("a::b";"::")
["a" "b"]
?> .split("a b";0c )
["a" "b"]
?> .split("abc";"")
error: .split: y must not be empty
?> .split(5;",")
error: .split: x must be a string, got integer

docs.title: .join
docs.text:
.join(x;y) [Join]

Return the strings of the list "x" joined, with the string or
character "y" between neighbours, as one string. The empty list
gives "". A member of "x" may be a character. A member of any
other type is a type error.

.join is the inverse of .split.

?> .join(["a" "b"];", ")
"a, b"
?> .join([];",")
""
?> .join(["a" 1];",")
error: .join: x must be a list of strings, got a list with integer

docs.title: .words
docs.text:
.words(x) [Words]

Return the non-empty pieces of the string "x" between runs of
white space (space, tab, newline and carriage return) as a list
of strings. A string with no words gives the empty list.

?> .words("  to be  or not ")
["to" "be" "or" "not"]
?> #.words("   ")
0

docs.title: .trim
docs.text:
.trim(x) [Trim]

Return the string "x" without the white space (space, tab,
newline and carriage return) at its start and end.

?> .trim("  a b  ")
"a b"

docs.title: .num
docs.text:
.num(x) [Number]

Return the number that the whole string "x" spells: an integer
or a real in Klong's number syntax, with an optional "-" before
it and optional white space around it. Return :undefined when
"x" is not exactly one number, e.g. "7 8", "x" or "".

Unlike .rs, which reads any data object and stops after the
first, .num accepts nothing else: .rs("7 8") is 7.

?> .num("12")
12
?> .num("-3.5")
-3.5
?> .num(" 7 ")
7
?> .num("7 8")
:undefined
?> .num("x")
:undefined
?> .num("")
:undefined
?> .num(5)
error: .num: x must be a string, got integer

docs.title: JSON
docs.text:
See JSON.

Name Title Description .json(x) JSON The JSON text of a Klong value (dictionaries to objects, lists to arrays, :undefined to null). .unjson(x) Un-JSON The Klong value of a JSON text (the inverse of .json); bad text is a range error with the position.

docs.title: .json
docs.text:
.json(x) [JSON]

Return the JSON text of the Klong value "x". A dictionary becomes
an object (its keys must be strings), a list or array becomes an
array, a number (an integer, a real, or a NumPy or torch scalar)
becomes a number, a string or a character becomes a string, and
:undefined, NaN and the infinities become null. The text has no
spaces after "," and ":". A symbol or a function is a type error
that says where it is.

.unjson is the inverse.

Example:

    .json(:{;"a";1;"b";[1 2 3]})

docs.title: .unjson
docs.text:
.unjson(x) [Un-JSON]

Return the Klong value of the JSON text "x": an object becomes a
dictionary with string keys, an array a list (an array of numbers
is an array; a list that holds an integer beyond 64 bits is a list
of objects, so that every integer stays exact), a string a string, a number an integer or a real,
true and false the integers 1 and 0, and null :undefined. Text that
is not exactly one JSON value (including NaN and Infinity) is a
range error that gives the line, column and character position.

.unjson is the inverse of .json, except that true and false are
read as 1 and 0.

Example:

    .unjson("{""a"":1,""b"":[1,2,3]}")

docs.title: Python and backend
docs.text: Name Title Description .py(x) Python Import a Python module and make its functions callable from Klong. .pyf(x;y) Python-From Import named functions from a Python module. .pya(x;y) Python-Attribute Return an attribute of a Python object, such as a function in an imported module. .pyc(x;y;z) Python-Call Call a Python function or method with positional and keyword arguments. .bkf(x) Backend-Function Import functions from the active backend's array module (NumPy or torch).

docs.title: .py
docs.text:
.py(x) [Python]

Import a python module in to the current context.  All methods exposed in the module
are loaded into the current context space and callable from within KlongPy.

If the string "x" refers to a directory, KlongPy will append __init__.py
to determine if the directory is a Python module and attempt to load the module.

If the string "x" ends with a .py, then KlongPy will attempt to load this file
as a Python module.

Example:

    Consider a Python package called greetings that exports the "hello" function:

        def hello():
            print("Hello, World!")

    This loads the package, as 'import greetings' does, and then calls 'hello',
    which prints Hello, World!

        .py("greetings")
        hello()

    Additionally, a full path to a module can be specified.  This can be useful for
    when creating custom modules that don't need to be installed into Python modules.

        .py("<path>/<to>/greetings")

docs.title: .pyf
docs.text:
.pyf(x;y) [Python-From]

Import the named functions of a Python module into the current context.

[See .py() for details on importing python modules]

Example:

    To import one function:

    .pyf("numpy"; "sqrt")
    sqrt(4) --> 2.0

    To import several:

    .pyf("numpy"; ["sqrt" "sin"])
    sin(1) --> 0.8414709848078965

?> .pyf("numpy";"sqrt");sqrt(4)
2.0

docs.title: .pya
docs.text:
.pya(x;y) [Python-Attribute]

Return the attribute named "y" of the Python object "x".

docs.title: .pyc
docs.text:
.pyc(x;y;z) [Python-Call]

Call a python function or class function with args and kwargs.

This is a utility function to allow for Klong programs to call Python classes,
or functions, with positional and keyword arguments.

x may be a list: the object symbol, then the name of the method to call.
x may also be a symbol that references the function name to call.

y is a list of positional arguments, or a single positional argument.
z is a dictionary of keyword arguments to pass to the function.

Example:

    Python objects may be directly called:

        .pyc(obj;[1 2 3];:{["a" 1] ["b" 2] ["c" 3]})

    or a method on the object may be called:

        .pyc(obj,"method";[1 2 3];:{["a" 1] ["b" 2] ["c" 3]})

    if the python object name is snake case, then the quote is not needed:

    Here, parse_date is a function in the iso8601 module:

        .pyf("iso8601";"parse_date")

    and it can be called via:

        .pyc("parse_date";,"2020-01-01";:{})

docs.title: .bkf
docs.text:
.bkf(x) [Backend-Function]

Import functions from the current backend's array module.
This is similar to .pyf() but uses backend-aware functions that
work with both numpy and torch backends.

When using the torch backend, these functions preserve gradient
tracking for autograd.

Example:

    .bkf("exp")
    exp(1.0) --> 2.718...

    .bkf(["exp" "sin" "cos"])
    sin(1.0) --> 0.841...

Common functions available: exp, sin, cos, tan, tanh, sqrt, abs,
log, log10, floor, ceil, round

?> .bkf("exp");exp(0.0)
1.0

docs.title: Strict mode
docs.text: Name Title Description .strict() Strict Turn on strict mode (level 1): a function may not create a global by assignment. .unsafe() Unsafe Turn strict mode off (level 0).

docs.title: .strict
docs.text:
.strict() [Strict]

.strict(x)

Set the strict level and return it. .strict() sets level 1;
"x" may be 0, 1 or 2. Level 0 is the default: see .unsafe().

Level 1: malformed input that level 0 only warns about (input
left after a statement, an unterminated string or list, a
missing operand) is a syntax error, and so is an assignment
whose left side is not a name. Inside a function, assigning to
a name that is not a declared local or an existing variable is
an error, and so is reading a name that is not defined.

Level 2: in addition, reading an undefined name is an error
everywhere, as is reading a local variable before it has been
assigned and passing more arguments than a function takes; a
quoted symbol (:a) is always the symbol, never the value of a
variable of that name.

The rule for :: is the same at every level: when a variable of
that name exists in any scope, it is assigned there. Otherwise,
at top level the variable is created; inside a function the
name becomes local to the call (level 0) or the assignment is
an error (level 1 and 2). To change a variable from a function,
define it at top level first. To create one from inside a
function, use .E.

Text is checked for syntax at the level in force when it is
read, and code runs under the level in force when it runs.

Example:
    .strict()
    counter::0
    increment::{counter::counter+1}  :" OK - counter exists"
    f::{newvar::42}
    f()  :" ERROR - undefined variable: newvar"
    g::{[t];t::42;t}
    g()  :" OK - t is declared local"

?> .strict()
1
?> f::{newvar::42}
:nilad
?> f()
error: undefined variable: newvar
?> g::{.E("newvar::42")}
:nilad
?> g()
42
?> newvar
42

docs.title: .unsafe
docs.text:
.unsafe() [Unsafe]

Set strict level 0, the default, and return 0. See .strict().

At level 0, assigning to a name that does not exist inside a
function makes the name local to that call. It does not create
a variable outside the function; use .E for that.

Example:
    .unsafe()
    f::{newvar::42}
    f()     :" 42; newvar is local to the call"
    newvar  :" still undefined"

?> .unsafe()
0
?> f::{newvar::42}
:nilad
?> f()
42
?> newvar
:newvar

docs.title: System variables
docs.text: Name Title Description .a Arguments Not defined in KlongPy; the program arguments are in .os.argv. .cin Input-Channel Standard input channel. .cout Output-Channel Standard output channel. .cerr Error-Channel Standard error channel. .cols Columns Screen width in columns. .e Epsilon Epsilon: 1+.e is 1.0 and .e is 1e-18 in KlongPy. .edit Editor Line editor switch. .fastpow Fast-Power Switch for compiling x^y to a faster power function. .h Host Symbol naming the host system (:unix or :plan9). .os.argv Program-Arguments The words after -- on the kgpy command line, as a list of strings. .os.env Environment The environment variables of the process, as a dictionary of strings.

docs.title: .a
docs.text:
.a [Arguments]

Not defined in KlongPy. The name is documented in the Klong manual; in KlongPy it evaluates to the symbol .a and has no effect. The program arguments are in .os.argv.

In the Klong manual this variable holds the command line
arguments of a program. KlongPy does not define it: the
arguments after "--" on the kgpy command line are in .os.argv.

docs.title: .cin
docs.text:
.cin [Input-Channel]

These variables are bound to the standard input (.cin), standard
output (.cout), and standard error (.cerr) channels of the Klong
process. They can be selected for input or output using the
From-Channel (.fc) and To-Channel (.tc) functions.

The standard I/O channels cannot be closed.

docs.title: .cout
docs.text:
.cout [Output-Channel]

See [Input-Channel]

docs.title: .cerr
docs.text:
.cerr [Error-Channel]

See [Input-Channel]

docs.title: .cols
docs.text:
.cols [Columns]

Not defined in KlongPy. The name is documented in the Klong manual; in KlongPy it evaluates to the symbol .cols and has no effect.

This variable stores the number of columns of the screen on
which the Klong session is running. It defaults to 80. This
variable is used by the line editor, if compiled in and enabled
(see .edit).

docs.title: .e
docs.text:
.e [Epsilon]

.e is the smallest value by which two real numbers (0.1<=x<1)
can differ. For numbers smaller than 0.1, there would be a
smaller difference and number x>=1 cannot differ by .e, because
1+.e --> 1. the actual value of .e is implementation-dependent.
In KlongPy it is 1e-18. Numbers are IEEE doubles, so the
spacing between neighbouring reals is about 1.4e-17 at 0.1 and
1.1e-16 just below 1; the statement above about the smallest
difference does not hold.

The logarithm to base 10 of %.e (ln(%.e)%ln(10)) equals the
number of digits in the mantissa of a real number (this is
exactly the exponent in the scientific notation of %.e).

KlongPy numbers are IEEE doubles, so the statement above about the smallest difference does not hold. .e is 1e-18, 1+.e is 1.0, and the spacing between neighbouring doubles is about 1.4e-17 at 0.1 and 1.1e-16 just below 1.

?> 1+.e
1.0
?> .e
1e-18

docs.title: .edit
docs.text:
.edit [Editor]

Not defined in KlongPy. The name is documented in the Klong manual; in KlongPy it evaluates to the symbol .edit and has no effect.

When this variable set to a true value AND the line editor is
compiled into the Klong executable, then line editing and
history will be enabled on the Klong prompt. See the section on
LINE EDITING for details.

docs.title: .fastpow
docs.text:
.fastpow [Fast-Power]

Not defined in KlongPy. The name is documented in the Klong manual; in KlongPy it evaluates to the symbol .fastpow and has no effect.

When this variable set to a true value, then expressions of the
form x^y will compile to .pow(x;y), which makes computations
involving powers of real numbers much faster (about eight times
on the author's hardware).

Setting .fastpow::0 will disable this feature and restore the
previous behavior of Klong, just in case.

docs.title: .h
docs.text:
.h [Host]

Not defined in KlongPy. The name is documented in the Klong manual; in KlongPy it evaluates to the symbol .h and has no effect.

This variable holds a unique symbol identifying the host system
running the Klong process. Currently, this is either :unix or
:plan9.

docs.title: .os.argv
docs.text:
.os.argv [Program-Arguments]

The words after -- on the kgpy command line, as a list of strings: the
empty list when there are none. kgpy sets it before the program runs, for
a file run, -e, -l and the REPL. A program that embeds KlongInterpreter
does not have it unless the host sets it.

kgpy script.kg -- 8888 AAPL runs script.kg with .os.argv equal to ["8888" "AAPL"]. Every word is a string: read a number with .rs, as in .rs(.os.argv@0). Words before -- are options of kgpy or the file name.

docs.title: .os.env
docs.text:
.os.env [Environment]

The environment variables of the process when kgpy started, as a
dictionary from name to value, both strings. kgpy sets it with .os.argv.

.os.env@"HOME" is the home directory. A name that is not set is a key error, so test with .os.env?"NAME" first.

docs.title: Timers
docs.text:
Defined in the base interpreter. See Timers.

Name Title Description .timer(x;y;z) Create-timer Call a function every y seconds (fractions allowed) until it returns 0 or the timer is cancelled. .timerc(x) Cancel-timer Cancel a timer.

docs.title: .timer
docs.text:
.timer(x;y;z) [Create-timer]

Create a timer named by "x" that calls the function "z" every "y"
seconds (fractions allowed) and returns its handle. An interval of 0
calls "z" at once, on the Klong loop. The result of the callback decides
what happens next: a false value (0, an empty list or string) stops the
timer, and any other value runs it again. The function takes no arguments
and is passed by name (cb::{...}; .timer("t";1;cb)): a function written
inline in the call is rejected, or run at the call site if it has no
arguments. A named function is looked up again on each tick, so a
redefinition takes effect. Stop a timer with .timerc, from any thread.

Example:

    n::0
    cb::{n::n+1;.p(n);:[n<3;1;0]}
    th::.timer("count";0.2;cb)

The interval y may be fractional. A negative, NaN or non-numeric y, or a z that is not a function, raises an error instead of returning a message string. If the callback raises, the timer is cancelled and stderr gets the line timer NAME callback failed; cancelling timer and the error. A timer fires while a file run is up for a server or a connection, but does not keep it up by itself (see Timer).

?> cb::{0}
:nilad
?> .timer("t";-1;cb)
error: y must be a non-negative number
?> .timer("t";"x";cb)
error: y must be a non-negative number
?> .timer("t";0.5;3)
error: z must be a function

docs.title: .timerc
docs.text:
.timerc(x) [Cancel-timer]

Cancel a timer created by .timer()

docs.title: IPC
docs.text:
Defined in the base interpreter. See IPC Capabilities.

Name Title Description .srv(x) Start-IPC-server Start the IPC server on a port or address; raises if the bind fails; .srv(0) stops it. .cli(x) Create-IPC-client Connect to a KlongPy IPC server and return a function that evaluates code remotely. .clid(x) Create-IPC-dict-client Connect to a KlongPy IPC server and return a dictionary backed by its variables. .clic(x) Close-IPC-client Close a connection opened by .cli or .clid. .async(x;y) Async-function-wrapper Wrap a function so that it runs asynchronously and calls a completion function. .cli.h Client-Handle The handle of the client whose request is being evaluated.

docs.title: .srv
docs.text:
.srv(x) [Start-IPC-server]

Listen for IPC connections. "x" is a port (all interfaces, 0.0.0.0), a
string "<bind>:<port>" for one interface, or 0 to stop the server and
drop its clients. Returns 1 when the server is now listening and 0 when
it was already started (for 0, when there was no server). If the port
cannot be bound, an error is raised. Clients speak the kdb+ IPC protocol.
Hooks, set as global functions: .srv.o(h) when a client connects,
.srv.c(h) when it disconnects, .srv.e(h;text) on an error that nobody
is waiting for, and .srv.auth(user;password), which returns 1 to
accept a client and 0 to refuse it. The .system key "ipc_max_message"
limits the message size (256 MiB by default). A 0.7 client (pickle
protocol, removed in 2.0) is closed at once and the cause is logged.

Security: a client can run any Klong code in this interpreter, and
credentials are sent in clear text. Bind to localhost, as in
.srv("127.0.0.1:8888"), and never expose the port to an untrusted
network. See the IPC Capabilities page.

Example:   .srv(8888)       -->  1

When the port cannot be bound (for example it is in use), .srv raises an error such as cannot listen on 0.0.0.0:8888: ... address already in use. A call over .cli or .clid that gets no reply within 30 seconds raises an error containing timed out, closes the connection, and fails any other call waiting on it. A synchronous call that this process would have to answer itself, such as a call to its own server from a file, a timer or a hook, is a system error at once: use .async. While a server listens, a file run does not end (see REPL and command line).

docs.title: .cli
docs.text:
.cli(x) [Create-IPC-client]

Connect to a server and return a function that runs code there. "x" is a
port (on localhost), "<host>:<port>", or "<host>:<port>:<user>:<password>"
(credentials travel in clear text); a remote dictionary from .clid shares
its connection. A string argument is Klong source for the server to run.
A symbol argument is the name of a server function, followed by its
arguments: f(:avg,,!100). A symbol alone returns the remote value, and
a remote function proxy for a function. The connection speaks the kdb+
IPC protocol, the only one; the pickle protocol of 0.7 was removed, and a
2.0 client cannot talk to a 0.7 server (the handshake times out).
A call waits 30 seconds at most (see .clit). An error on the server is
raised here as the error of its kind. If nothing listens on the port,
.cli blocks for about 155 seconds, then returns the function, and the
first call through it is a system error. See the IPC Capabilities page.

Example:   f::.cli(8888)
           f("1+1")         -->  2
           f(:avg,,!100)    -->  49.5

docs.title: .clid
docs.text:
.clid(x) [Create-IPC-dict-client]

Connect to a server and return a dictionary of its variables. "x" is
an address as for .cli, or a remote function from .cli, whose
connection is shared. Setting a key sets a global on the server, and a
get of a name the server does not have is a name error. A function set
on the server is read back as a remote function proxy. The protocol,
timeout and errors are those of .cli.

Example:   d::.clid(8888)
           d,[:foo 2]       -->  sets :foo to 2 on the server
           d?:foo           -->  2

docs.title: .clic
docs.text:
.clic(x) [Close-IPC-client]

Close a remote dictionary or function opened by .cli or .clid.

Returns 1 if closed, 0 if already closed.

When a connection is closed, all remote proxies / functions tied to this connection
will also close and will fail if called.

docs.title: .async
docs.text:
.async(x;y) [Async-function-wrapper]

Returns an async functional wrapper for the function "x" and calls "y"
when completed. The wrapper has the same arity as the wrapped function.
Both must be functions, else a type error is raised.

Calling the wrapper returns 1 at once. A local function runs as a task on the
Klong loop and "y" is called with its result. When "x" is a connection (from
.cli) or a remote function proxy, the request is sent without blocking
and "y" runs on the Klong loop when the answer arrives; an error answer or a
lost connection is logged and "y" is not called. With a connection the
wrapper takes the one request argument, as the connection does.

docs.title: .cli.h
docs.text:
.cli.h [Client-Handle]

While a request of a client is evaluated, the handle of that client
(as .srv.o and .srv.c are given it); undefined at any other time.

docs.title: Autograd
docs.text:
Defined in the base interpreter; most need the PyTorch backend. See PyTorch Backend and Autograd.

Name Title Description .jacobian(x;y) Jacobian Jacobian of a function at a point. .gradcheck(x;y) Gradcheck Check autograd gradients against numeric ones (PyTorch backend). .export(x;y;z) Export Export a function's computation graph to a file (PyTorch backend).

docs.title: .jacobian
docs.text:
.jacobian(x;y) [Jacobian]

Compute Jacobian matrix of function x at point y.

For f: R^n -> R^m, returns m x n matrix where J[i,j] = df_i/dx_j.

Examples:
    f::{[x@0^2 x@1^2]}
    .jacobian(f;[1 2])   -->  [[2 0] [0 4]]

docs.title: .gradcheck
docs.text:
.gradcheck(x;y) [Gradcheck]

Verify that autograd gradients match numeric gradients.
Uses torch.autograd.gradcheck for rigorous verification.
Requires the torch backend (kgpy --backend torch, or KlongInterpreter(backend="torch")).

Arguments:
    x       - Function to check (should return a scalar)
    y       - Input value or list of inputs to check

Returns:
    1 if gradients are correct
    Raises error if gradients don't match

Examples:
    f::{x^2}
    .gradcheck(f;3.0)            :" Returns 1

    g::{(x@0^2)+(x@1^2)}
    .gradcheck(g;[1.0 2.0])      :" Returns 1

Notes:
    - Only supported with PyTorch backend
