A chip below revision v3.0 needs another build (CONFIG_ESP32P4_SELECTS_REV_LESS_V3=y in sdkconfig.defaults), and the bootloader refuses this image on such a chip.

Task klong, pinned to CPU 1, priority 1, 128 KiB stack in internal RAM. The runtime is given a budget of 120 KiB (Config::for_stack), so deep recursion is a range error and not a crash Heap in PSRAM (MALLOC_CAP_SPIRAM); the limit is three quarters of the free PSRAM (about 24 MiB) with a reserve of 16 KiB; without PSRAM, 256 KiB of internal RAM Console the ESP-IDF UART driver on UART0 with a 32 KiB receive buffer; raw bytes, no echo or line buffering by ESP-IDF; the runtime sends CR LF Logging switched off at the start of app_main; only the boot log comes before the banner. A panic (a bug, or a watchdog) still prints and restarts the board Clock esp_timer_get_time Idle feeds the task watchdog (30 s, panic) and sleeps 1 ms .x() esp_restart, which is how the conformance runner gets a fresh interpreter per case Files a RAM file system in the same heap; uploads are lost at reset. Flash storage is not done Features files, lib, timers; no IPC (this firmware does not use the transports that the C interface offers, a UART link called a lane; see Porting to a Board)

docs.title: Building the firmware
docs.text:
You need Docker with the ESP-IDF image that build.sh pins (ESP-IDF v5.5.4), and stable Rust with the target of the P4:

rustup +stable target add riscv32imafc-unknown-none-elf
cd native/boards/esp32p4
./build.sh

build.sh does two things. It builds libklong_ffi.a for riscv32imafc-unknown-none-elf (release, with LTO) into native/target/esp32p4/, and then it runs idf.py -DIDF_TARGET=esp32p4 build and idf.py size in the container, with native/ mounted. The output is in native/boards/esp32p4/build/: bootloader/bootloader.bin, partition_table/partition-table.bin, klong_esp32p4.bin and flash_args. For a clean build, remove build/ and sdkconfig.

The Rust target is riscv32imafc and not the more common riscv32imac because every ESP-IDF build for the P4 uses the ilp32f calling convention, and the linker refuses to mix it with the soft-float objects of riscv32imac-unknown-none-elf. The C interface passes only integers and pointers. Doubles are computed in software on both sides (the P4 has single-precision hardware only).

The image klong_esp32p4.bin is 691,328 bytes in a partition of 1.5 MB, so 55 percent of the partition is free. The bootloader is 23,072 bytes and the partition table 3,072. The Rust library is about 481 KB of the image. It is built with the speed optimisation level (opt-level 3) and not for size, since flash is not scarce on this board.

docs.title: Flashing
docs.text:
Check the chip first. The image is for revision v3.1 or later and 32 MB of flash:

esptool --chip esp32p4 -p PORT chip-id
esptool --chip esp32p4 -p PORT flash-id

Then, from native/boards/esp32p4 (esptool 5; write-flash @flash_args from the build/ directory does the same, which is what build.sh suggests when it ends):

esptool --chip esp32p4 -p PORT -b 460800 --before default-reset --after hard-reset \
    write-flash --flash-mode dio --flash-freq 80m --flash-size 32MB \
    0x2000 build/bootloader/bootloader.bin \
    0x8000 build/partition_table/partition-table.bin \
    0x10000 build/klong_esp32p4.bin

PORT is the serial device of the board, for example /dev/ttyUSB0 on Linux or /dev/cu.usbserial-110 on macOS. This overwrites the bootloader, the partition table and the first application partition of whatever was on the board. Back the flash up first if that matters.

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
Open the port at 115200 8N1 with no flow control, with any terminal program that opens a serial device. Two things are worth knowing before you do.

  • Opening the port resets the board. The USB-serial bridge toggles DTR and RTS, which reset the chip, so you see the boot log every time you open the port. A program that holds the board's state in RAM loses it. The upload tool waits for the banner after it opens the port.
  • After a reset the first line you send can fail with input is not valid UTF-8. A stray byte arrives with or after the boot, and the console takes it into the line you type. Known limit: press Enter once, or Ctrl-C, and type the line again. The current main.c discards the receive buffer before it prints the banner (drain_rx).

docs.title: What you see
docs.text:
After the boot messages of the ROM, the bootloader and ESP-IDF, the board prints the banner and the prompt:

Klong 0.0.1 (esp32p4, int64 float64)
klong>

From here it is the console described on the Serial Console and Upload page, with the line editor, the history and the continuation lines. The board does what that page shows: expressions are evaluated, an error shows its position and the prompt returns, .l("nstat") loads the embedded library, and a runaway loop such as {1}{x+1}:~0 is stopped by Ctrl-C with an interrupt error.

Integers and floats are 64 bits wide in this firmware (int64 float64 in the banner); the P4 has single-precision floating point hardware only, so doubles are computed in software. fib(24) (f::{:[x<2;x;f(x-1)+f(x-2)]};f(24)) took 4.2 seconds on the board, and about 35 ms on a desktop (Apple M2 Ultra), a factor of about 120. The program uses integers only. Known limit: the cause of the difference has not been investigated, and the board's speed is not measured beyond that one figure.

A call of a Klong function costs about 28 us (4.2 s over the 150,049 calls of fib(24)), about 10,000 cycles at 360 MHz.

docs.title: Uploading a file
docs.text:
The tool is native/tools/kgupload.py, which uses only the Python standard library. On a board it works as on the simulated one, and it opens the port at 115200 baud, the speed of the console (--baud N changes that; at another speed the board does not answer):

python native/tools/kgupload.py PORT ver
python native/tools/kgupload.py PORT upload hello.kg
python native/tools/kgupload.py PORT run -e '.l("hello.kg")'

The first command prints the version line: widths, features, platform name, fs=1, the free heap and the console limits. The second stores hello.kg in the RAM file system of the board; for a UTF-8 text file it uses the put command and for any other file Intel HEX, with a check of the CRC-32 either way. The third runs a program on the board, here one that loads the file you stored. All subcommands and options are on the console page. A transfer that is cut off leaves the old file in place.

Because the file system is in RAM, the file is gone after a reset, which includes opening the serial port again and .x(0). A file that the board should have after power-up has to be uploaded again each time. A boot.kg on the file system runs before the banner, but since the file system is empty at power-up, that is only useful once flash storage exists.

If the board is slow to boot, the first command waits for the banner; give it a longer --timeout.

docs.title: Running the conformance suite over the wire
docs.text:
native/scripts/console_conformance.py runs the cases of the conformance suite on the board. For each case it resets the board with .x(0), waits for the banner, sets the strict level if the case has one, and sends the program with ^A run; it compares the value, the console output and the kind of the error with the case:

python native/scripts/console_conformance.py --port PORT --baud 115200

This gave 1266 of 1266 on the ESP32-P4, in 1877 seconds (about 31 minutes). Most of the time goes into the reset and boot of the board before each case: that is about 1.5 seconds per case. With a firmware built with int32 and float32, add --narrow so that the cases for that build are chosen. The sysio cases write files; on a board without storage you would leave them out with --tags, and here they run against the RAM file system.

The runner needs .x to really reset the board, a banner within --timeout and a max_run of at least the largest case, which holds for this firmware.

docs.title: What has not been done
docs.text:
• IPC and the management node on this board, .cli, .srv: this firmware has no transport for them. The C interface has transports (the lane feature, which the Pico firmware uses), but the ESP32-P4 firmware does not use them. IPC has run on two Picos, and on a desktop over TCP. See IPC and Timers and Management Node.
  • Flash storage. Files live in RAM and are lost at reset.
  • The stack and heap on the board. The firmware's numbers (a budget of 120 KiB of the 128 KiB stack, a heap limit of three quarters of the free PSRAM) come from the porting rules and the build; how much a level of recursion costs on this chip, how the heap behaves in PSRAM under load, and whether the 30 second task watchdog is long enough for the longest single operation, have not been measured.
  • The receive path at speed. Whether bytes are lost during long evaluations at 115200 baud with the 32 KiB buffer is not known beyond the conformance run, which passed.
  • Why fib(24) is slow, as said above. The current source builds ESP-IDF's C with -O2 and serves the small blocks that a call allocates from free lists in internal RAM; fib(24) with it has not been measured.
  • The thumbv7em target and the other boards. The code links for thumbv7em-none-eabihf and riscv32imac-unknown-none-elf, but those images have no start-up code and were never booted. The same main.c ran for an ESP32-C3 under QEMU, which is not hardware: it booted and ran expressions, uploads, timers and .x. Known limit: a runaway loop there ends in an interrupt watchdog timeout, and the cause is not investigated.

docs.title: IPC and Timers
docs.text:
This page covers the network and timer functions of the native Klong runtime: .srv, .cli, .clid, .clic, .clit, .async, the .srv.* hooks, .timer and .timerc. It shows a native runtime and KlongPy calling each other in both directions, says how far compatibility with q and kdb+ has been tested, states the trust model, and lists the limits and the differences from KlongPy. It is for people who want a native node to talk to KlongPy or to a q process.

The functions are the same ones, with the same names and the same wire protocol, as in KlongPy, so read IPC Capabilities for the value mapping, .cli proxies, .clid, callbacks and the hooks in full. This page does not repeat that page. It covers what is different on the native side.

Trust model

A peer that connects to a native node can run any Klong code on it. With the file functions built in, it can read and write that node's files. There is no encryption and no TLS. A user name and password given to .cli travel in clear text, and .srv.auth only checks them, so it is a convenience and not a defence. Listen only on an isolated or trusted network, bind to 127.0.0.1 when you can, and never expose the port to an untrusted network. This is the same model as KlongPy's (see the security model in the README). It is also true of a management node, which controls every node behind it: see Management Node.

docs.title: Where it runs
docs.text:
Where State The kg program on the desktop, over TCP built in and tested: with KlongPy in both directions, native to native, and against PeachQ (a kdb+-compatible q implementation) The simulated board klong-sim built in (.ver() lists ipc), but it has no transport: .srv and .cli answer system error: this platform has no tcp transport An ESP32-P4 not built in. The firmware has no IPC, and the ESP32-P4 has run no IPC (see the status table). The C interface has one transport, the lane (a UART link of 16-byte frames; klong-ffi --features lane), and the ESP32-P4 firmware does not use it The nodes of a packet switch that carries 16-byte frames, .cli("node:2") built in as the node transport; proven in the simulator and run on two Picos (2026-11-16): see two Picos calling each other Links over a UART, or a lossy packet radio the code is there and was tested in memory with seeded faults (see below); on a wire it has run only on the UART link between two Picos

The kg program registers one transport, TCP, and the examples on this page use it. The C interface has the lane transport (klong-ffi --features lane), which carries IPC over a UART link of 16-byte frames and the Pico firmware uses; a board port can supply another.

docs.title: The functions
docs.text:
Function Does .srv(ADDR) start listening; returns 1. ADDR is a port, or the string "bind:port" for one interface .cli(ADDR) connect; returns a function that evaluates a string there, or calls a symbol with arguments .clid(c) the remote context as a dictionary (shares the connection when given one from .cli) .clic(c) close a connection; returns 1, or 0 if it was not open .clit(c;seconds) set the call timeout of a connection (default 30; 0 for none) .async(f;cb) call f, then cb with the result, without waiting .srv.o, .srv.c, .srv.e, .srv.auth hooks you define: a client opened, a client closed, an error nobody waits for, and the login check .cli.h inside a function run for a client, the handle of that client's connection .timer(name;seconds;fn), .timerc(handle) a repeating timer, and stopping it

Addresses are as in KlongPy:

Address Meaning 8888 port 8888 on localhost (for .srv: every interface) "host:8888" port 8888 on host "host:8888:user:password" the same, with a user name and password "tcp:host:8888" the same as "host:8888", with the transport named "name:address" any other transport that the platform has, with its own address; .cli("uart:1@921600") is how the management example in Management Node names a UART. The kg program has only tcp

An address that is not one of these is a type error (bad address a:b: expected a port or "host:port"). A .srv on a port that is taken is a system error (cannot listen on 127.0.0.1:8888: address in use).

docs.title: A native server and a KlongPy client
docs.text:
The block starts a native node that serves two functions and prints a line when a client arrives and when it leaves, then runs a small KlongPy client file. kgpy -l runs the file and goes on to the REPL; the REPL sees an empty standard input and leaves, and sed keeps the first four lines of output, which are the client's. kgpy FILE, without -l, stays up while the file holds an open connection, until Ctrl-C or .clic (the REPL), so the example uses -l.

$ kg -e 'sq::{x*x};total::{+/x};.srv.o::{.p("client connected")};.srv.c::{.p("client left")};.srv("127.0.0.1:8888")' > server.log 2>&1 & echo $! > server.pid; for i in $(seq 600); do [ -s server.log ] && break; sleep 0.1; done
$ cat > client.kg <<'EOF'
> c::.cli("127.0.0.1:8888")
> .p(c(:sq,,7))
> .p(c("1+2"))
> .p(c(:total,,!101))
> f::c(:sq)
> .p(f(12))
> .clic(c)
> EOF
$ kgpy -l client.kg | sed -n 1,4p
49
3
5050
144
$ for i in $(seq 100); do [ $(wc -l < server.log) -ge 3 ] && break; sleep 0.1; done; cat server.log; kill $(cat server.pid)
1
client connected
client left

Reading the client: c(:sq,,7) calls the symbol :sq with the argument list [7] (,7 is the one-element list), c("1+2") evaluates a string on the server, and f::c(:sq) asks for the remote function itself, a proxy that you call as if it were local. The first line of server.log is the 1 that .srv returned. The server evaluated each request in its own interpreter, and it printed the two hook lines itself.

One trap, the same in KlongPy: a symbol that names a function defined on the caller's side is that function. With sq defined on both nodes, c(:sq,,7) and f::c(:sq) send the caller's own sq for the peer to apply (the way c(inc,1) sends the source of inc), not a call of the peer's. To call the peer's function whatever you have defined, send the list c([:sq 7]) or the string c("sq(7)"), and for .async give it the handle, af::.async(c;cb), and call af([:sq 7]).

docs.title: A KlongPy server and a native client
docs.text:
The other direction. The KlongPy node runs in the background for up to 25 seconds (sleep 25 | keeps its REPL from seeing the end of its input, and the file kgpy.pid holds its process number so that the last command can stop it), and the native klong is the client. kgpy -s 8888 serves port 8888 and -l loads a file first.

$ printf 'sq::{x*x}\nmean::{(+/x)%%#x}\n' > server.kg
$ sleep 25 2>/dev/null | kgpy -s 8888 -l server.kg > kgpy.log 2>&1 & echo $! > kgpy.pid; for i in $(seq 600); do lsof -nP -iTCP:8888 -sTCP:LISTEN >/dev/null 2>&1 && break; sleep 0.1; done
$ kg -e 'c::.cli(8888);.p(c(:sq,,7));.p(c(:mean,,[1 2 3 4]));c("1+2")'
49
2.5
3
$ printf 'c::.cli(8888)\nc(:nosuch,,1)\n' | kg 2>&1 | grep -v '^ *$'
  :monad
  1:1: name error: symbol not found: nosuch
  c(:nosuch,,1)
  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  hint: reported by localhost:8888
$ kill $(cat kgpy.pid)

An error on the server comes back as an error of the same kind on the caller, and the hint line says which peer reported it. Both runtimes do this for every error kind of the language, and for remote, the kind of an error that a q peer signalled.

docs.title: Calls that do not wait
docs.text:
.async(f;cb) sends the request, returns 1, and runs cb with the answer when it arrives. Native callbacks run from the event loop, never inside an evaluation that is waiting. With -e the program keeps running after the last statement while an answer is still due, so the callback prints:

$ printf 'sq::{x*x}\n' > server.kg
$ sleep 25 2>/dev/null | kgpy -s 8888 -l server.kg > kgpy.log 2>&1 & echo $! > kgpy.pid; for i in $(seq 600); do lsof -nP -iTCP:8888 -sTCP:LISTEN >/dev/null 2>&1 && break; sleep 0.1; done
$ kg -e 'c::.cli(8888);g::.async(c(:sq);{.p("got ",$x)});g(6);.p("sent")'
sent
"sent"
got 36
$ kill $(cat kgpy.pid)

The answer to g(6) came after sent: the call did not wait. An error in an asynchronous call does not call cb. It is logged on the caller's error channel as .async: remote call failed: ....

docs.title: Timeouts, logins and refused connections
docs.text:
A call that takes longer than the connection's timeout fails with a system error, and the connection is no longer usable (open a new one). A server that is busy evaluating moves no bytes meanwhile, so it looks dead to its peers for that long.

$ kg -e 'wait::{[t];t::.pc()+x;{.pc()<t}{x}:~0;x};.srv("127.0.0.1:8888")' > w.log 2>&1 & echo $! > w.pid; for i in $(seq 600); do [ -s w.log ] && break; sleep 0.1; done
$ printf 'c::.cli(8888)\n.clit(c;0.5)\nc(:wait,,2)\n' | kg 2>&1 | grep -v '^ *$'
  :monad
  1
  1:1: system error: call timed out after 0.5s: localhost:8888
  c(:wait,,2)
  ^^^^^^^^^^^
$ kg -e 'c::.cli(8888);.p(c(:wait,,0.2))'
0.2
"0.2"
$ kill $(cat w.pid)

A server that defines .srv.auth checks the user name and password in the address. A wrong or missing login is refused during the handshake, and the client's error says so:

$ kg -e '.srv.auth::{(x~"ann")&y~"pw"};sq::{x*x};.srv("127.0.0.1:8888")' > a.log 2>&1 & echo $! > a.pid; for i in $(seq 600); do [ -s a.log ] && break; sleep 0.1; done
$ kg -e 'c::.cli("127.0.0.1:8888:ann:pw");c(:sq,,5)'
25
$ kg -e 'c::.cli("127.0.0.1:8888:bob:no");c(:sq,,5)' 2>&1 | sed -n 1p
1:4: system error: 127.0.0.1:8888 closed the connection during the handshake (bad credentials, or it does not speak the kdb+ protocol)
$ kill $(cat a.pid); sleep 1
$ kg -e '.cli(8888)' 2>&1 | sed -n 1p
1:1: system error: cannot connect to localhost:8888: connection refused

(The user name and password are sent in clear text; this example is exactly what the trust box warns about.) Connecting does not return at once to a host that does not answer: the TCP transport waits at most 5 seconds in connect.

docs.title: Timers
docs.text:
.timer(name;seconds;fn) starts a repeating timer and returns a handle. seconds may be fractional. fn is called with no arguments every interval; its result decides what happens: 0 stops the timer, anything else continues. .timerc(handle) stops a timer and returns 1, or 0 if it was not running. A callback that fails cancels its timer, and the error is written to the error channel as timer NAME callback failed; cancelling timer: ....

$ kg -e 'n::0;cb::{n::n+1;.p(n);:[n<3;1;0]};.timer("count";0.2;cb)'
:timer
1
2
3

As with a server, kg stays alive while a timer runs, so the program above ended on its own when the callback returned 0. In the REPL, timers and the IPC connections are served while the REPL waits for a line.

Time on a native node is cooperative. Nothing fires while an evaluation or a blocked IPC call runs. A timer that came due meanwhile fires once afterwards and then at its next multiple of the interval, counted from its start. A timer is not a way to run work at an exact moment.

KlongPy and native differ in one respect. KlongPy looks up a named callback again at each tick, so redefining cb changes what a running timer calls. The native .timer keeps the function value it was given. After cb::{.p("old");1} and .timer("t";0.2;cb), a later cb::{.p("new");0} changes what a KlongPy timer prints from old to new, and leaves the native timer printing old. The library of the management node avoids the difference by passing a function that calls a name: {mgmt.tick()}.

docs.title: Events, one task
docs.text:
All of this runs on the one task that evaluates Klong code. A client call sends its request and then loops: move bytes, take the next event of that connection, and serve it if it is a request, until its own answer arrives, its timeout passes or the console sends Ctrl-C. That is why a server function can call back into the client that is waiting for it (the .cli.h handle, as in KlongPy), and why calls can nest. The nesting is limited to 8 levels, and the 9th is answered with an error (nested calls deeper than ...). Requests that arrive while nothing waits are served from the event loop, one per connection at a time, in arrival order.

Ctrl-C on the console ends a blocked call and closes that connection.

While a call waits, the node does nothing else: no timer fires and other clients wait. This matters for the management node, which waits for its nodes.

docs.title: Compatibility with q and kdb+
docs.text:
The native runtime speaks the kdb+ IPC protocol, as KlongPy does: the handshake, the framing, the type codes, little endian, compression understood (capability 3), compression of what is sent when it pays. A q client library can connect to .srv and send a string or call a function by name, and .cli can connect to a q process.

What was tested: the codec against 119 shared test vectors (decode, reject, round trip byte for byte), through both the codec and the session. And, with the process tests of tests/test_native_ipc.py, a native client with PeachQ 0.92.20261115 (a third-party, kdb+-compatible implementation of q) as the server, and PeachQ's hopen as a client of a native .srv. The tests run only when the environment variable KLONG_TEST_PEACHQ names a PeachQ executable. Those 11 tests are skipped by default. The runtime has not been tested against a KX kdb+ process. What a kdb+ server prints or accepts that PeachQ does not is not known.

docs.title: Differences from KlongPy
docs.text:
KlongPy native A list that mixes integers and floats object array arrives as a float array Dictionary keys from a peer any numbers, chars, strings and symbols; a list as a key is a type error for that one message, and the connection stays up A symbol longer than 255 bytes range error for that message Bytes that are not valid UTF-8 in a string replaced by U+FFFD replaced by U+FFFD (strings are always valid text) An error signalled by q with a bare name (type, length) kind remote kind remote .timer with a named callback looked up at every tick the function value given is kept Tables Built-in tables and the Python table adapter can send and receive keyed and unkeyed tables Desktop builds with tables can send and receive both forms Connect blocks, with retries that can take minutes against a host that does not answer blocks at most 5 seconds Two interpreters in one process allowed not on two threads at once (the nesting bound and a deferred-failure flag are per process)

The error kinds an error takes on the way: each kind of the language arrives as the same kind on the other side, so a range error on a native server is a KlongRangeError in KlongPy and a range error again when it travels on to another native node. The remote kind is new in the native runtime, as it is in KlongPy.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Message size. The default limit is 256 MiB, which is a figure for a desktop. A device sets it from its heap: decoding takes about 1 to 2 times the message for a vector and, at worst, about 70 bytes of heap per byte of message for a dictionary of bytes. A 1,000,000-element float array was sent each way between KlongPy and native.
  • Nesting. Values nest at most 64 levels on the wire, calls at most 8.
  • Memory per connection. About 1 to 2.5 KB of heap per connection, plus one read buffer shared by all connections (64 KiB on a 64-bit host, 1 KiB on a 32-bit target) and the message being received. native/scripts/ipc_bench.py measured on 2026-11-16 2149 bytes per idle connection on a server and 2303 on a client, and 66 KB left over after 100 connections had closed.
  • Symbols from peers are never freed. A peer can grow the symbol table; the heap limit bounds it.
  • Speed. One megabyte of integers echoed over localhost TCP took 1.95 ms per round trip between two native nodes, 1.97 ms from KlongPy to native, 1.42 ms from native to KlongPy and 1.35 ms from KlongPy to KlongPy (the same script, 20 repetitions, on one desktop; the figures are indicative and differ between machines). A native node polls its sockets without being told they are ready and sleeps between polls.
  • Known limit: a port in the OS's ephemeral range. .cli("localhost:PORT") tries the addresses localhost has in order, the IPv6 one first. With nothing listening there and PORT among the ports the OS gives to outgoing connections, a socket can be given PORT as its own port and connect to itself (TCP's simultaneous open), and then reads its own greeting as the server's: bad capability byte in the server's reply. The host transport refuses a connection whose two ends are the same address, and goes on to the next address.
  • A long evaluation moves no bytes. A peer on a packet link sees no acknowledgements meanwhile, and with the keepalive on, an evaluation longer than the keepalive budget looks like a dead link.
  • Callbacks within one process. Two runtimes on one thread cannot call each other, because each waits for the other. Calls between processes nest as described.

docs.title: Links that are not TCP
docs.text: The IPC code does not do I/O itself. A platform supplies transports, and the runtime puts a reliability layer on any link that is not a reliable stream. For a UART there is a framing with COBS and a CRC-16, and over it a go-back-N layer with a window of 16 packets and a retry budget. These were tested in memory, with seeded loss, duplication and reordering of 1 to 30 percent and with damaged bytes. At 30 percent a stream arrived intact only with a retry budget raised from 8 to 16, and with 100 percent loss the session fails with a timeout after 8 retransmissions. A CRC-16 cannot make "never delivers a corrupted value" absolute: a damaged frame passes with a probability of about 1.5 in 100,000. The COBS and CRC-16 framing has not run on a real UART (the two-Pico link uses the 16-byte frames described below), and the kg program cannot reach these transports, so the process tests are all TCP. See Porting to a Board for what a board supplies.

docs.title: Links that carry messages, not bytes
docs.text: A packet link does not have to be a serial line. If the network delivers bounded messages (a radio, a switch, a bus with frames), a platform makes a PacketLink over it: mtu is the largest message, send and recv move one message, and the same reliability layer runs on top. An IPC message larger than the network's message is not a problem and not an error: it is part of the byte stream that the layer cuts into packets. The link may also give the layer timeouts that suit it (PacketLink::tuning: handshake timeout, retries, keepalive), because the defaults assume a link of some KB/s or more. The one such network so far is a switch of 16-byte frames with 4 bytes of payload, whose largest message is 1024 bytes. It carries 2.9 KB/s on 115200 baud lanes and 112 KB/s at 4.5 Mbaud. .cli("node:2") connects to node 2 over it, with the kdb+ bytes unchanged. Two Picos have run it; see two Picos calling each other.

docs.title: Management Node
docs.text:
This page covers the mgmt library (klongpy/lib/mgmt.kg), which turns one node into a management node: it keeps a registry of other nodes, checks that they are alive, relays calls to one node or to all of them, and stores source files on them. It is for people who run several native Klong nodes and want one place to reach them from. It is the role that a baseboard management controller has in a server, and it is not tied to any board.

Trust model

Anyone who can reach the management node can run any code on it and on every node behind it, and can read and replace the files of each of them. Nothing is encrypted, and .srv.auth sees a user name and a password that travel in clear text. Let the management node listen on an isolated or trusted network only, preferably on 127.0.0.1 or a private link. This is the trust model of IPC and Timers, made larger: one connection to the management node is a connection to all of them.

What has been run

Most of this page ran on one computer: the nodes and the management node are kg processes that talk over localhost TCP, and a second set of tests runs several runtimes in one thread over simulated lossy and serial links. On hardware, the library has loaded and management-library calls (mgmt.call) have run between two Raspberry Pi Picos (see two Picos calling each other). Not run on a board: a management board with nodes on UARTs, and a pulled cable. The hooks node.reset and node.power (below) are a place for a board to plug into, and no board does yet. The status table has the one summary.

docs.title: The pieces
docs.text:
desktop (KlongPy or kg)  --.cli-->  management node  --.cli-->  node n1
                                         (mgmt library)   --.cli-->  node n2
                                                          --.cli-->  node n3

A node is any runtime that serves IPC: a native kg with .srv. A node needs nothing installed. When the management node connects, it defines three names on the node (mgmt.run, mgmt.job and mgmt.r) and nothing else, and it writes nothing to the node's storage unless you ask it to.

The management node loads the library with .l("mgmt"). The native runtime carries the file in its image when it is built with the ipc feature, so no file is needed there. KlongPy finds it on its library path.

Nodes are named by strings and reached by transport address strings, the ones .cli takes. The library never looks inside an address, so a node can be at "127.0.0.1:5001", "tcp:10.0.0.11:5000" or "uart:1@921600" on a platform that has that transport.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
Call Does mgmt.add(name;address) register a node and try to connect to it; a name that is already there gets the new address mgmt.nodes the registry, a dictionary from name to :{["addr" a] ["h" handle or 0] ["state" s] ["seen" t] ["ver" v] ["wait" w] ["t" n]} mgmt.names() the names, in the order they were added mgmt.status() name to :{addr state seen age ver}: the registry without the handles mgmt.timeout(name;seconds) the call timeout of one node mgmt.start(seconds) check every node now, and then every seconds mgmt.stop() stop checking mgmt.open(name) connect a node now (again, if it already has a link) mgmt.call(name;fn;args) call fn on a node with the list args, and return the result mgmt.each(names;fn;args), mgmt.all(fn;args) the same call on several nodes at once, and on all of them: a dictionary from name to the result or to an error value mgmt.put(name;path;text) write a file on a node; returns the number of characters written mgmt.boot(name;text) write the node's boot.kg, which it runs when it starts mgmt.load(name;path) have the node load a file now (.l(path) there) mgmt.reset(name), mgmt.power(name;on) call node.reset(name) and node.power(name;on), when this board defines them; otherwise name error: mgmt: this board has no node.reset

Settings: mgmt.ct is the call timeout a node gets when it is added (30 seconds), mgmt.pi is the interval that mgmt.start was given, and mgmt.probe is the request a check sends (".ver()"). The defaults are provisional. In mgmt.nodes, state is "up" or "down", seen is the .pc() time of the last answer (-1 before the first), ver is what .ver() gave there, wait is 1 while a probe is unanswered, and t is the node's call timeout.

fn is a symbol (the node's function of that name), a string (source that the node evaluates; give a function literal such as "{+/x}", and with args of [] the value of the source is the result), or a function (sent as its source). Passing a string like "+/x" that is not a function literal does not apply it to args.

docs.title: A worked example
docs.text:
Three nodes, a management node in front of them, and a desktop client, all on localhost. The commands are run from one shell. The ports are 8888 for the first node and the next ones above it, and 8891 for the management node; the checker of this documentation replaces 8888 with a free port.

Start three nodes. Each defines sq and serves one port:

$ for i in 1 2 3; do kg -e "sq::{x*x};.srv(\"127.0.0.1:$((8888+i))\")" > n$i.log 2>&1 & echo $! > n$i.pid; done; for i in $(seq 600); do [ -s n1.log ] && [ -s n2.log ] && [ -s n3.log ] && break; sleep 0.1; done

Write the management node's program. It registers the nodes, starts the liveness check every 0.3 seconds, defines one helper, and serves the management port. The ports are the arguments of the program, which a file reads from .a:

$ cat > mgr.kg <<'EOF'
> .l("mgmt")
> mgmt.add("n1";"127.0.0.1:",.a@0)
> mgmt.add("n2";"127.0.0.1:",.a@1)
> mgmt.add("n3";"127.0.0.1:",.a@2)
> mgmt.start(0.3)
> states::{{(mgmt.nodes?x)?"state"}'mgmt.names()}
> .srv("127.0.0.1:",.a@3)
> EOF
$ kg mgr.kg $((8888+1)) $((8888+2)) $((8888+3)) $((8888+10)) > mgr.log 2>&1 & echo $! > mgr.pid; for i in $(seq 600); do lsof -nP -iTCP:$((8888+10)) -sTCP:LISTEN >/dev/null 2>&1 && break; sleep 0.1; done; cat mgr.log

The management node prints nothing. kg stays alive because a timer runs and a server listens.

Now the desktop. A client connects to the management node with .cli and sends it requests: a string to evaluate, or a list whose first element is the symbol of a function. The mgmt functions are called through the management node, so the list [:mgmt.call "n2" :sq [7]] is a request to call mgmt.call("n2";:sq;[7]) there. The client is another klong here; it could be KlongPy.

$ cat > desk.kg <<'EOF'
> m::.cli("127.0.0.1:",.a@0)
> .p(m("mgmt.names()"))
> .p(m([:mgmt.call "n2" :sq [7]]))
> .p(m([:mgmt.all :sq [6]]))
> .p(m("states()"))
> EOF
$ kg desk.kg $((8888+10))
[n1 n2 n3]
49
:{[n1 36] [n2 36] [n3 36]}
[up up up]

mgmt.call relayed the call to n2 and returned 49. mgmt.all sent the request to all three nodes before waiting for any answer, so they computed at the same time, and returned a dictionary of the results. The helper states shows the registry entries. The list literal [:mgmt.call ...] is how the library itself takes symbols, because symbols in list literals are never looked up as variables. At strict levels 0 and 1 a quoted symbol is the value of a variable of that name when there is one, so a desktop that has its own sq and writes :sq outside a list literal sends its function and not the name.

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
mgmt.put writes a file on a node, and mgmt.load has the node load it. All three nodes run in this directory, so the file shows up here:

$ cat > deploy.kg <<'EOF'
> m::.cli("127.0.0.1:",.a@0)
> .p(m([:mgmt.put "n2" "cube.kg" "cube::{x*x*x}"]))
> m([:mgmt.load "n2" "cube.kg"])
> .p(m([:mgmt.call "n2" :cube [3]]))
> r::m([:mgmt.all :cube [2]])
> .p(r?"n2")
> .p((r?"n1")?"message")
> EOF
$ kg deploy.kg $((8888+10))
13
27
8
n1: undefined function: cube
$ cat cube.kg
cube::{x*x*x}

mgmt.put returned the 13 characters it wrote. The call of cube on n2 gave 27. mgmt.all gave 8 for n2 and, for the two nodes that never loaded the file, an error value, which does not stop the others: its message starts with the node's name. mgmt.boot(name;text) writes boot.kg the same way. A board runs its boot.kg when it starts; the host kg does not, so to bring a node back with it you start it as kg boot.kg.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
An error on a node is raised on the management node as an error of the same kind, with the name of the node in front of the message, and it travels on to the desktop with that kind:

$ printf 'm::.cli(%s)\nm([:mgmt.call "n1" "{1+x}" ["a"]])\n' $((8888+10)) | kg 2>&1 | sed -n 2p
  1:1: type error: n1: cannot apply + (Plus) to integer and string

A link that fails, and a call that times out, are system errors that start with the node's name. Errors of the management node itself start with mgmt:. In a fan-out, mgmt.each and mgmt.all do not raise: a dead node or a slow one becomes an error value in the result, and costs at most its own timeout, because the requests go out to every node first and each node has until its own deadline. The error value is a dictionary:

:{["error" kind] ["node" name] ["message" text]}

Klong has no error type, so a node whose own answer is such a dictionary cannot be told from a failed one.

docs.title: Liveness
docs.text:
Every interval each node is sent mgmt.probe without waiting. An answer makes the node "up". A node that has not answered by the next check is "down", and so is one whose link failed or whose call timed out; the check connects it again at the following check. Kill a node and the check notices:

$ kill $(cat n3.pid); sleep 1.2
$ cat > after.kg <<'EOF'
> m::.cli("127.0.0.1:",.a@0)
> .p(m("states()"))
> r::m([:mgmt.all :sq [6]])
> .p(r?"n1")
> .p(r?"n3")
> EOF
$ kg after.kg $((8888+10))
[up up down]
36
:{[error system] [node n3] [message n3: not connected]}

With the check running, a fan-out does not connect a node that has no link. It reports not connected at once and leaves connecting to the check. Without that, a node that accepts a connection and then says nothing would hold every fan-out for the handshake time (5 seconds, not settable from Klong). A node that is busy for longer than the interval is reported "down" until it answers: an evaluation moves no bytes. A killed process is reported at the next check; a link that goes silent, at the check after the unanswered probe, so up to two intervals. If you want the node back, start it again on the same port; the next check connects it and marks it up.

While mgmt.call or a fan-out waits, the management node does nothing else: no check runs and other clients wait. One evaluation at a time.

Last, stop what the example started:

$ for f in mgr n1 n2; do kill $(cat $f.pid); done

docs.title: .try and .err
docs.text:
The library needed two functions that Klong did not have: a way to catch an error and a way to raise one. They are one pair, and they are functions, not statements (a program raises with .err and catches with .try, and what one catches the other raises again). Both are in kg, in kgpy and on every board build, from the same runtime.

.try(f;args) applies the function f to the list args. The result is [1 result] when it worked and [0 e] when it raised an error. e is a dictionary, as every collection of named things is in Klong (principle 3 of the design principles):

Entry Value "kind" the name of the error kind, a string: syntax, name, arity, type, shape, range, system, memory, internal or remote (the kinds of Errors) "message" the message, a string "source" the name of the program text the error was found in (a file name, <-e>, <stdin>), or "" "line", "col" where, counting from 1; 0 when the error has no place

An interrupt (Ctrl-C, .x) is not caught. .err(kind;message) raises an error of that kind with that message, for any kind except interrupt, and the kind may be a string or a symbol. .err(e) raises what .try caught, with its kind and its message (the place it reports is that of the .err; the place of the first failure is in e). A program that wants a category of its own writes it in the message: the kinds are the language's.

$ kg -e 'f::{x+"a"};.try(f;,1)'
[0 :{["kind" "type"] ["message" "cannot apply + (Plus) to integer and string"] ["source" "<-e>"] ["line" 1] ["col" 6]}]
$ kg -e 'g::{x+1};.try(g;,1)'
[1 2]
$ kg -e 'f::{x+"a"};e::(.try(f;,1))@1;e@"message"'
"cannot apply + (Plus) to integer and string"
$ kg -e 'f::{x+"a"};e::(.try(f;,1))@1;.err(e)'
1:30: type error: cannot apply + (Plus) to integer and string
  f::{x+"a"};e::(.try(f;,1))@1;.err(e)
                               ^^^^^^^
$ kg -e '.err("range";"bad index")'
1:1: range error: bad index
  .err("range";"bad index")
  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
$ kg -e '.err("interrupt";"stop")'
1:1: range error: .err: interrupt is not an error kind
  .err("interrupt";"stop")
  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A function literal with no argument, written as the argument of a user function, is evaluated on the spot: that is the rule of the language (f::{x+1};f({41}) gives 42, because f receives 41). As the function argument of .try, .async or .timer it stays a function, so .try({1+"a"};[0]) catches the error that the function raises, and .timer("t";1;{0}) hands .timer the function. To pass such a function to a user function, give it a name or an argument:

$ kg -e 'h::{1+"a"};.try(h;[0])'
[0 :{["kind" "type"] ["message" "cannot apply + (Plus) to integer and string"] ["source" "<-e>"] ["line" 1] ["col" 6]}]
$ kg -e '.try({x;1+"a"};[0])'
[0 :{["kind" "type"] ["message" "cannot apply + (Plus) to integer and string"] ["source" "<-e>"] ["line" 1] ["col" 10]}]

The management library keeps the older, flat form on the wire between nodes, [1 result] or [0 kind message], so that a node of either age understands another; mgmt.cfg.trap says whether the runtime has .try (1) or not (0), and it is worked out the first time it is needed.

The two functions cost about 1.7 KB of flash on thumbv7em-none-eabihf and 2.3 KB on riscv32imac-unknown-none-elf (older figures); the dictionary of the caught error adds a little code.

docs.title: KlongPy as the management process
docs.text:
The file loads in KlongPy at every strict level and is tested there (TestKlongPyAsManagementNode in tests/test_native_mgmt.py), with native nodes behind it. A native client can drive it through .srv. What works:

  • the registry, and mgmt.call with values of every type;
  • mgmt.all and mgmt.each when every link is up (an error on a node is still an error value, because the node catches it);
  • mgmt.put, mgmt.boot, mgmt.load;
  • the liveness check marking a killed node down.

What differs:

  • mgmt.add does not connect; the first call does.
  • An error of a node keeps its kind but does not carry the node's name.
  • A link that fails or a node that is too slow during a fan-out fails the whole call.
  • The check does not connect a node again; mgmt.open(name) does. The reason is that .cli in KlongPy blocks for minutes when nobody listens at the address.
  • An error of the management node itself is a name error about mgmt.error, after the message is printed.
  • At strict level 2 KlongPy cannot be asked whether .try exists, so set mgmt.cfg.trap::0 yourself after loading the library (mgmt is a module and cfg is its dictionary of settings).

The nodes behind it are native runtimes in every case.

docs.title: Limits and what is not done
docs.text:
• Resources. A load reads one statement at a time and keeps functions as their text. On the 64-bit host the library needs a heap of about 43 KiB to load, peaks at about 40 KB in all and holds about 18 KB more afterwards (.mem()). On a Pico it keeps about 10 KB in use (two Picos calling each other). It is 12.6 KB of text in the image, of which about half is the header that is also in this page. A 32-bit build has not been measured.
  • Defaults. The probe interval of 5 seconds in the library's example and the call timeout of 30 seconds are provisional. The keepalive of the packet layer and the probe do similar jobs, and one of them may be enough on a real UART.
  • Reconnect. A node comes back only at a check, so a management node without mgmt.start does not reconnect a node by itself; mgmt.open(name) does.
  • Hooks. node.reset and node.power are looked up by name when called. No board defines them.
  • No Python helper. There is no klongpy.mgmt class; the client side is .cli to the management node, as above.
  • Boards. The reference configuration (a management board with nodes on UARTs), the behaviour with a pulled cable, a node's boot.kg run at power-up after mgmt.boot, and the heap and flash of a real management board have not been tried. See ESP32-P4: that firmware has no IPC.

docs.title: Two Raspberry Pi Picos calling each other
docs.text: Two Raspberry Pi Pico boards (RP2040, 264 KiB of RAM) ran the native Klong interpreter and called each other over IPC. For other targets, see the board status table.

docs.title: The setup
docs.text:
Each Pico has one UART lane on GP16 (TX) and GP17 (RX) of uart0, configured at 4.5 Mbaud, 8N1, with no flow control. The two lanes are joined through a switch that forwards fixed 16-byte frames, each carrying up to 4 bytes of payload. A supervisor board numbers the nodes and reads their status. The framing permits at most 112.5 kB/s of payload before acknowledgements and higher-level protocol overhead.

The two-Pico result used a serial switch of 16-byte frames that is not part of this repository. Its frame format is in native/boards/pico-bench/README.md and klong-sim models it. The firmware, the simulator and the host tools are in the repository. Without the switch you can run the same runtime and self-test in the simulator and drive a node from your own frame source, but you cannot reproduce the measured two-board numbers. To set up a link of your own:

  • The node transport needs any byte link between two UARTs and something that numbers the nodes. A node learns its number from the destination of the first frame it receives.
  • The simulator in native/klong-sim models the switch, with a clock for each lane, and runs the same runtime and the same self-test. klong-bench runs it from a script.
  • native/tools/klong_bench.py is a console client for the nodes. native/tools/bench_bridge_sim.py serves the same interface in front of the simulator, so the client runs without any hardware.
  • tests/test_native_pico_pair.py runs two nodes of the firmware's own allocator behind a model of the switch.

IPC over the lane is the ordinary kdb+ protocol. A reliability layer (handshake, sequence numbers, go-back-N retransmission) sits between it and the datagrams that carry it, as for any serial link. An address is node:N: .cli("node:2") connects to node 2 and .srv("node:") accepts connections from any node. See IPC and Timers for the functions.

Two nodes in the simulator, one serving and one calling. The time is virtual and includes the connection and 60 ms in which the nodes learn their numbers:

$ klong-bench 2 --baud 4500000 <<'EOF'
> 1> sq::{x*x};.srv("node:")
> 0> h::.cli("node:1");h(:sq,,7)
> time
> EOF
1: 1
0: 49
t = 0.066 s

docs.title: Build the firmware
docs.text:
You need stable Rust with the thumbv6m-none-eabi target, CMake, Ninja, the Pico SDK 2.x and the Arm GNU toolchain. Then:

native/boards/pico-bench/build.sh

The result is build/klong_pico_bench.uf2 in that directory. The two RP2040 boards used the same image. native/boards/pico-bench/README.md lists the build settings and the pins.

At boot every node serves. A node that is not number 0 connects to the nearest node below it that answers and runs a self-test: a call, an asynchronous call, a 4 KB echo, and the management library calling the peer. The verdict is reported to the supervisor as text and as status flags.

docs.title: RC1 on two RP2040 boards
docs.text:
The November 20, 2026 run used a sealed KlongPy 2.0.0rc1 build (source archive SHA-256 beginning 547dd7b9). Both boards booted UF2 image SHA-256 2e89418263b298b8644725a0f238ead6d8c182778f824dfa97bf8abe29bc09f0 and returned 2.0.0-rc.1 from .ver() over the lane. The raw firmware binary was 809,252 bytes.

Check RC1 observation Paired boot Node 2 served five calls. Node 3 passed in 615 ms, including a 95 ms echo of 500 integers. A controlled reboot passed in 616 ms. IPC A plain remote evaluation returned 42 in both directions, with about 5 ms per call after the connection opened. Three management calls returned 2 and took 30, 15 and 14 ms. Compiled C Moving average and PID agreed with the interpreter on both boards. FIR agreed with all 241 reference values in flash. See On a Pico for the workloads and timings. Interrupt and recovery Each node reported an interrupt on the lane and then evaluated 3+4 to 7. Recursion and recovery For the tested recursive function, both boards returned 113 at depth argument 113 and reported a range error at 114. Both evaluated 1+2 after a deeper call failed. Largest integer vector after reset After 16 seconds idle, #!5951 on the self-test client (node 3) and #!6826 on the serving node (node 2) succeeded. The next size failed on each. Largest integer vector with management loaded On node 2, after one successful management call and two seconds idle, #!5060 succeeded and #!5061 returned a memory error. Largest integer vector after mixed use After compiled examples, recursion and IPC, node 2 reached 3,386 and node 3 reached 4,473.

The physical run exercised the UART lane console. Direct Pico USB CDC prompt and Ctrl-T counter checks were deferred, and this run provides no direct USB upload result. The current checkout's stack-budget fix and boot self-test memory cleanup passed host regressions and built together for RP2040. The follow-up image has not been flashed.

docs.title: Earlier measurements
docs.text:
Measure Result Image About 650 KB for the November 17 measurements (430 KB with KLONG_OPT=z). The November 18 image with compiled examples, string functions and static-profile declarations used 734 KB of flash. Boot self-test, both boards started together 0.52 s Largest integer vector on the node that ran the self-test 5,500 Largest integer vector on the serving node, management library loaded 5,500 Loading the management library (.l("mgmt")) 0.16 s; about 10 KB stay in use once it has been used A call to the other node through the library, first 26 ms The same call, repeated in one program 11 ms for one call; ten calls in one request take 84 ms A plain .cli call, no library 3.4 ms A 4 KB echo 94 ms fib(18), 8,361 calls 0.39 s Recursion depth 105 levels; the 106th is a range error and the node goes on Compiled C on both boards (.c.check(), November 18) Moving average and PID were about 100 times faster than their interpreted versions. FIR was checked against reference values from a desktop. See On a Pico.

Conditions: two boards, 2026-11-17, through the console client, one firmware image (Pico SDK 2.3.1, Arm GNU 15.3.1); the plain .cli call was measured on an earlier firmware image. Each vector size is the largest of the sizes tried, in steps of 300 to 500 elements.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
The default stack reservation is 112 KiB. The receive and transmit rings use 16 KiB and 8 KiB respectively, and the evaluator's hot functions also run from RAM. The RC1 linker map showed 56,344 bytes for static data and code in RAM, 99,304 bytes between the static area and the stack, and 114,688 bytes for the stack. The runtime's allocation limit reported by .mem() was 93,160 bytes.

The allocator tends to place small blocks near the top and vectors and parse trees near the bottom. A large vector needs a contiguous block and enough headroom under the runtime's allocation limit. After the controlled management call on RC1, node 2 had 50,368 bytes free in its pool, with a largest free block of 40,480 bytes. The limit also reserves room for the evaluator to report an allocation error.

Functions from a loaded file are kept as text. Calling one parses it again from that text and keeps the tree in a cache of 24 entries. A program that calls many functions pays a parse for each, which is why the first call through the library is slower than the repeated ones.

.heap(mode) reads the heap back. It is a diagnostic in the build by default; KLONG_HEAP_DIAG=0 ./build.sh leaves it out.

Call Returns .heap(0) 32 integers: pool size, bytes in use, the peak, free bytes, the largest free chunk, counts of free chunks and requests refused, and the addresses of the pool and of the stack .heap(1), .heap(2), ... pages of runs of the pool in address order: offset, size, free or used, kinds of the blocks .heap(100), ... pages of live blocks of 512 bytes or more: offset, size, kind .heap(200) the cached small blocks, by size class .heap(300), .heap(301) restart the high-water mark; read the heap near it

.mem() gives [in use, peak, limit] as the runtime counts them.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• Available contiguous memory depends on what the node has loaded and run. Use .heap(0) and .mem() to inspect the current pool and the runtime's counted usage.
  • The boot self-test clears its mgmt binding. Run .l("mgmt") before using mgmt.add from the console.
  • The stack budget depends on the build and the call path. The recursion results above describe the tested function.
  • Sustained bidirectional lane traffic still needs measurement. The USB console's Ctrl-T report includes rx ring overruns for diagnosing receive losses.
  • The RP2040 performs floating-point arithmetic in software. The compiled workloads above use single precision, and this interpreter build uses double precision.

docs.title: Run the host tools
docs.text:
Everything below runs without a Pico:

cd native && cargo build --release          # klong-bench, klong-sim
python native/tools/bench_bridge_sim.py --port 18751 --nodes 2 &
python native/tools/klong_bench.py --host 127.0.0.1:18751 status
python native/tools/klong_bench.py --host 127.0.0.1:18751 eval --node 1 'sq::{x*x};sq(12)'

tests/test_native_pico_pair.py, tests/test_native_bench_cli.py and cargo test --release -p klong-sim run the pair, the client and the simulator.

docs.title: Porting to a Board
docs.text:
This page is a summary of what it takes to run the native Klong runtime on a new board: what a port has to supply, the C interface that lets a vendor SDK application drive the runtime, and how much flash and RAM to plan for. It is for someone who has a microcontroller and wants to know what the work is before reading the header that defines the C interface, native/klong-ffi/include/klong.h. native/PORTING.md in the repository has the notes for a port in Rust.

Two kinds of board have run the runtime: the ESP32-P4 and two Raspberry Pi Picos. The images for thumbv7em-none-eabihf and riscv32imac-unknown-none-elf link but have never been booted. The Picos are Cortex-M0+ (thumbv6m-none-eabi). The status table says what has run where, and the last section here lists what only a new board can show.

docs.title: What a port is
docs.text:
The runtime does not know what chip it runs on. A port gives it a few services, and the runtime supplies everything else: the interpreter, the system functions, the serial console with its line editor and upload protocol, timers, and (where the board has a transport) IPC.

Piece Crate Does a port touch it? klong-core the language, no_std no klong-rt the Platform and FileSystem traits, system functions, timers, IPC, heap accounting implements its traits klong-console the serial console: prompt, line editor, ^A commands no klong-board the skeleton of a port: Uart, Clock, System, BoardPlatform, run, an allocator, a linkable image copies or uses it klong-ffi the same runtime as a static library with a C interface links it klong-sim a board that is not there: the console over memory, a pipe or a pseudo-terminal no (it is the test bench) tools/kgupload.py the desktop side of upload and run no

There are two ways in. If the board's firmware is written in Rust, implement the traits of klong-board and call klong_board::run. If the firmware is a vendor SDK application in C (ESP-IDF, the Pico SDK), link libklong_ffi.a and fill a configuration structure with callbacks. The ESP32-P4 port does the second; its glue is a single file of about 200 lines, native/boards/esp32p4/main/main.c.

docs.title: What a port supplies
docs.text:
A serial port (Uart, or the read and write callbacks).

  • read returns the bytes that have already arrived, and 0 when there are none. It must not wait. The runtime polls it from the main loop and, during an evaluation, every 4096 steps, a few milliseconds at most. That poll is how Ctrl-C stops a running program, so no interrupt handler has to know about Ctrl-C.
  • write sends all the bytes; it may wait for the transmitter.
  • The receive buffer must hold what arrives between two polls. At 115200 baud that is 12 bytes per millisecond. The runtime itself keeps at most 4096 bytes of typed-ahead input during an evaluation and drops the rest.
  • During a flash write a board may be unable to receive. Either give the UART a buffer for the longest write, or let the sender pace itself (kgupload.py --chunk and --chunk-delay), or use hex uploads, where the sender never runs more than --window records ahead of the acknowledgements.
  • The console is never used for IPC. IPC needs a transport of its own.

A clock (Clock, now_ms): monotonic milliseconds or microseconds. The upload timeout (5 seconds) and the timers use it, and a clock that stands still means a stalled transfer never times out. wall_clock (seconds since 1970) is optional.

System services (System, the optional callbacks):

Callback Does If absent name the board's name for the banner, .ver() and ^A ver required, at most 31 bytes idle called every turn of the main loop and every 4096 steps of an evaluation: feed the watchdog, yield to the RTOS; must be cheap nothing wait(max_ms) sleep until input may have arrived or until the deadline; returning early is always right the loop runs busy reset(code) .x(code): restart the chip .x only stops the program entropy 64 random bits to seed .rn() the clock is used fatal the runtime cannot go on (a Rust panic, which is a bug); the message is not terminated the runtime loops forever

reset matters more than it looks. The conformance runner uses .x(0) to get a fresh interpreter for each case, so without a real reset the cases share one interpreter and some fail.

Storage (optional): a klong_rt::FileSystem with open read write seek close remove rename list. The upload protocol needs Mode::Write to create or empty a file, Mode::Update to keep the content and allow writing anywhere, a seek past the end followed by write to leave a gap that reads as zero (Intel HEX records arrive in any order), and a rename that replaces an existing file (uploads go to PATH.tmp first). write may return fewer bytes than given, but not 0. klong_rt::memfs::MemFs, a RAM file system, is the reference for the contract and what the C interface provides. Without storage, put and hex answer err system, run works, and .l loads only the built-in library. LittleFS or FAT is the port author's choice; none is done.

Memory settings. Two numbers and a limit:

  • stack_bytes: the native stack the interpreter may use, measured from the frame that calls klong_run. Deep recursion beyond it is a range error, not a stack overflow.
  • the heap: a pair of alloc and free callbacks (or an allocator over a region), a heap_limit, and a heap_reserve of 8 to 16 KiB held back so that running out is a memory error at the prompt. The runtime counts the bytes it asks for, so the limit has to leave room for the allocator's own overhead (three quarters of the free PSRAM on the ESP32-P4).
  • The interrupt flag and the allocator's counters are static variables: they must be in internal RAM. On Xtensa, atomics in PSRAM do not work.

docs.title: The C interface
docs.text:
The interface is the header native/klong-ffi/include/klong.h, which has KLONG_ABI_VERSION 1. Only integers and pointers cross it, never a float or double, so the header means the same under a soft-float and a hard-float C ABI. Everything runs on one task: nothing in it is reentrant or thread-safe, and every call and every callback happens on that task.

Function Does int32_t klong_init(const klong_config *config) build the runtime, run boot.kg if the file system has one, print the banner Klong VERSION (NAME, int64 float64) and the first prompt. The config is copied. Returns KLONG_OK (0), KLONG_ERR_ARG (-1: null config, wrong ABI version or size, a required callback missing) or KLONG_ERR_STATE (-2: already initialised) int32_t klong_step(void) one turn of the main loop: console input, then timers. 1 when something was done, 0 when there was nothing to do (the caller may sleep), -1 before klong_init void klong_run(void) the main loop: klong_step, and the wait callback when there was nothing to do. Returns only if klong_init was not called void klong_heap(size_t *used, size_t *peak, size_t *limit) heap figures in bytes; any pointer may be NULL void klong_set_diag(size_t (*diag)(uint32_t mode, int64_t *out, size_t cap)) a diagnostic of the heap, in a library built with the cargo feature heapdiag (the Pico bench): the board's function fills the integers of a mode and the system function .heap(mode) returns them; the runtime also says what each allocation is for in volatile uint8_t KLONG_ALLOC_TAG. See the Pico page

The configuration structure, klong_config:

Field Meaning abi_version, size KLONG_ABI_VERSION and sizeof(klong_config); both are checked ctx passed back as the first argument of every callback alloc(ctx, size, align), free(ctx, ptr, size, align) the heap; align is a power of two, 8 for 64-bit numbers, so a 4-byte aligned malloc is not enough heap_limit, heap_reserve the limit in bytes (0 for none) and the reserve heap_overhead, heap_round what the allocator keeps per block (its header) and the grain it gives blocks out in, so that what the runtime counts is what the arena holds (0, 0: the sizes asked for) grow(ctx, ptr, old_size, new_size, align) optional: resize a block where it is (1 if done, 0 if not, and then nothing has changed). A vector that grows by doubling then needs the room it grows by and not the old block and the new at once; without it the runtime allocates, copies and frees stack_bytes as above; 32 KiB is the least that is useful write(ctx, bytes, len), read(ctx, buf, cap) the console, raw bytes both ways: no echo, no line buffering, no CR LF translation by the driver now_ms(ctx) monotonic milliseconds idle, wait, reset, entropy, fatal the optional services above name the board's name, at most 31 bytes, copied flags KLONG_FLAG_CRLF (send CR LF for LF, as a terminal on a UART expects), KLONG_FLAG_DUMB (no echo, no editing, no history), KLONG_FLAG_NO_FS (no RAM file system: put and hex fail, run works)

A sketch of the glue, from the ESP32-P4 port (not a complete program; the callbacks are the parts you write):

klong_config cfg = {
    .abi_version = KLONG_ABI_VERSION, .size = sizeof cfg,
    .alloc = k_alloc, .free = k_free, .heap_limit = heap_bytes, .heap_reserve = 16 * 1024,
    .stack_bytes = task_stack - 8 * 1024,
    .write = k_write, .read = k_read, .now_ms = k_now_ms,
    .idle = k_idle, .wait = k_wait, .reset = k_reset,
    .name = "myboard", .flags = KLONG_FLAG_CRLF,
};
if (klong_init(&cfg) == KLONG_OK) klong_run();

Two more functions are in the library built with the feature cfun (the Pico bench): klong_cfun_register(name, arity, fn, ctx, out_cap) defines a system function that runs a C function, and klong_extern_register(symbol, fn, ctx, out_cap) provides the C function a program declares with adc::.extern("read_adc";"int -> float"). The extern is keyed by its C symbol and is not a global: a program reaches it only through the function .extern returned, which checks the arguments and the result against the signature. It may be registered before or after the program declares the symbol.

What a module is and where .l looks for a name are decided in one place, native/klong-core/src/module.rs (scan, interface, search), which is no_std and is part of the core every board links. The runtime (klong-rt's modules.rs) calls it with the platform's file system and the library of the image; the linter and the checker call the same functions with the disk.

The C interface has the features files, lib and timers. IPC needs a transport from the platform. The C interface has one, built with klong-ffi --features lane: the functions klong_lane_init, klong_lane_pump, klong_lane_node and klong_lane_stats_get of klong.h. A lane is a UART link that carries 16-byte frames, to a switch or a peer node. Over it the library provides IPC (.cli("node:2"), .srv("node:")) and a console channel. The Pico firmware is a C application that uses it (two Picos). The ESP32-P4 firmware does not, and has no IPC. The C interface has no other transport, such as TCP. A port in Rust can provide any transport (Platform::transports()) and then calls poll_events from its loop.

docs.title: Memory budgets
docs.text:
Flash. The image of klong-board, linked with the size profile (opt-level = "z", LTO, panic = "abort"), for the two bare-metal targets that link. Measured on 2026-11-16 (bytes; see Building and Running for how):

Target Features .text .rodata flash thumbv7em-none-eabihf files, lib 176,788 72,656 249,464 files, lib, int32, float32 162,564 72,440 235,024 no files, no lib 167,188 29,676 196,884 riscv32imac-unknown-none-elf files, lib 218,990 109,092 328,102 files, lib, int32, float32 205,518 107,984 313,522 no files, no lib 207,056 63,664 270,740

These include the console. Static RAM (.data and .bss) is 48 bytes beside the heap. The Klong library is about 42 KiB of .rodata (the lib feature). IPC adds roughly 42 KB on thumbv7em and 59 KB on riscv32imac, timers 1.7 and 2.5 KB, the mgmt library 12.6 KB, and .try and .err 1.7 and 2.3 KB (older figures). The ESP32-P4 image is 691,328 bytes flashed; it is built with the speed profile and includes ESP-IDF.

The images of the board skeleton, linked with the min-size profile (cargo +stable build -p klong-board --profile min-size), measured on 2026-11-18. The first column is the console and the embedded library (files, lib, ipc, timers), the second the same with int32,float32, the third no console and no default features (no files, no library, no IPC):

Target Console Console, 32-bit No console, bare thumbv7em-none-eabihf 315,876 299,996 236,964 riscv32imac-unknown-none-elf 418,192 401,072 326,510 thumbv7em-none-eabihf before the module system (.l of a module, export, a.b) 300,948 285,032 226,916

The module system costs 12.5 KB on the console image and 7.7 KB on the bare one (the image without files or library has no .l: the loader is not built there, which saves 1.4 KB). By part, on thumbv7em with the console: the loader of the runtime 4.0 KB, the module scopes and their release in the core 2.1 KB, qualified names a.b 1.1 KB, the lookup and assignment rules 1.4 KB, the parser 0.6 KB, the library files written as modules 1.5 KB of text, the rest in what the other changes pull in. .try, .err (the error as a dictionary), .seed, .now and reading a qualified name on a host value add 2.4 KB to the console image, 2.3 KB to the 32-bit one and 2.4 KB to the bare one (1.0 KB net of the loader that the bare image no longer has).

RAM.

  • The console keeps 432 bytes of state (32-bit) inside the board's main structure. On the heap it takes at most max_line (1024) for the line, history_bytes (2048) for 32 lines of history, max_entry (8192) while a multi-line entry is open, 4096 for typed-ahead input, and max_run (64 KiB) only while a program sent with run is held. put and hex stream to the file system through a 128-byte buffer. The limits are fields of ConsoleConfig; a board with a small heap lowers max_run and max_entry.
  • The interpreter needs about 12 KiB after start-up (about 15 KiB on the 64-bit host in the transcripts of Building and Running). 1+1 needs 1.5 KiB more, a dictionary of 100 entries 26 KiB, a load reads one statement at a time and keeps functions as their text, so .l("csv") peaks at about 29 KB, .l("math") at about 139 KB, .l("mgmt") at about 40 KB and .l("nstat") at about 322 KB (see Building and Running). Parsed source costs 20 to 30 bytes of heap per byte of source.
  • Practical floors: 64 KiB of heap runs expressions and small programs (the whole conformance suite but one case); 256 KiB runs the whole suite; about 350 KiB covers the largest library file, nstat.
  • Stack. 32 KiB or more for the interpreter task. A level of Klong recursion costs about 0.85 KiB of native stack on a 32-bit target (864 bytes measured on a Pico). At the default of keeping a quarter of the budget back, 16 KiB gives about 14 levels, 64 KiB about 57 and 256 KiB about 228. Deeper recursion ends as a range error. On the simulated board (klong-sim --stack-budget) the console conformance suite passes all but one case with a 64 KiB stack and all but two with 32 KiB; the misses recurse deeply. On the ESP32-P4 the budget is 120 KiB; the Pico firmware has a 112 KiB stack, tells Klong it may use 108 KiB (4 KiB stay for the frames above), keeps 16 KiB of that and reaches 105 levels.

docs.title: Bring-up, in short
docs.text:
The steps:

  1. Build the core for the target with cargo build -p klong-board --lib --profile min-size --target TRIPLE (stock Rust for Arm and RISC-V; the Espressif fork for Xtensa).
  2. Write and test the UART alone: echo bytes, send 4 KiB in one burst and count them back. Write the clock and check it against a stopwatch for a minute.
  3. Start with no file system and a static heap, call klong_run, and expect the banner and klong>.
  4. Check +/!100 (4950), editing and history, and that f::{f(x+1)};f(0) is a range error, !100000000 a memory error, and {1}{x+1}:~0 runs until Ctrl-C and then says interrupt. The prompt must survive each.
  5. Let the runaway loop run for longer than the watchdog period before Ctrl-C.
  6. Add storage and test kgupload.py PORT upload and a 1 MB binary; pull the plug during an upload and check that the old file is still there. Test a stalled transfer: ^A put f 100 0 and send nothing gives err system: transfer timed out after 5 seconds.
  7. Check that boot.kg runs before the banner.
  8. Run the conformance suite through the console and record the count, the time and heap_peak from ver: python native/scripts/console_conformance.py --port PORT --baud 115200. See Serial Console and Upload.

If the board resets when the serial port is opened (DTR and RTS on ESP32 development boards), the upload tool's first ver waits for it to boot; raise --timeout if the boot is slow.

docs.title: What only a board can show
docs.text:
These were not and could not be checked on a host:

  • that the image boots: start-up code, linker script, vector table, clock setup, and a -march that matches the silicon. The images for thumbv7em and riscv32imac have none of these, and are not bootable (the Pico firmware supplies them for thumbv6m);
  • UART behaviour at speed: overruns during evaluation and during flash writes, the highest reliable baud rate, whether flow control or pacing is needed;
  • the real stack use per recursion level on the target, and so the right stack_bytes;
  • the allocator on real RAM: PSRAM mapping, fragmentation over days, and whether the heap limit leaves the SDK what it needs;
  • the flash file system against the FileSystem contract: seek past the end, rename over a file, power loss during an upload;
  • watchdog and RTOS behaviour of idle and wait, soft-float f64 speed, timings;
  • reset through .x, and whether opening the serial port resets the board.

The ESP32-P4 has answered the first group: the image boots, the console works, Ctrl-C stops a runaway loop, uploads work and the conformance suite passes over the wire. The flash file system and power loss are untested anywhere, because that board's storage is RAM.

The known weak spots of the protocol are listed on the console page.
